title: Day and night: how the spinning Earth makes them

summary.text: The Sun never stops shining. When it is night here, our side of the Earth has simply turned away from it. The Earth is a huge ball that spins once in about 24 hours. Half of it always faces the Sun and has day. The other half has night. The spin carries every place into the light and out again. That is why the Sun seems to rise in the east and set in the west. We cannot feel the spin, but a swinging pendulum, the stars turning round the Pole Star and photos from space all show it. The spin is very slowly getting slower. Scientists are still working out the details of how the Earth first got its spin.
summary.art: A blue Earth ball lit from one side by a bright Sun, half in daylight and half in night, with a small curved arrow showing the spin and a tiny child standing on the line between light and dark.

intro.hook: Right now, as you read this, you are moving faster than an aeroplane. You are not in a car or a train. You are sitting still. So how can that be?
intro.text: In most of India, the ground under your feet is moving at about 1,500 kilometres an hour. A passenger jet flies at about 900. Your house, the trees, the air and you all move together, so you feel nothing. In the afternoon here, it is night for children in America, and their Sun has not gone anywhere. Their side of the Earth is facing away from it. So why can't we feel the Earth spin, and how does the spin give us day and night?
intro.art: A child sitting still on a chair on a rooftop in an Indian town, with speed lines behind the whole town and a faint giant curve of the Earth below, the Sun low on one side.

outcomes: I can explain that day and night happen because the Earth spins, so each place turns towards the Sun and then away from it.
I can show day and night with a ball and a torch, and say why half of the Earth always has day.
I can explain that the Sun only seems to move across the sky, rising in the east and setting in the west, because the Earth turns from west to east.
I can say that one whole spin takes about 24 hours, and read the time of sunrise, noon and sunset on a clock.
I can explain why places further east, like Arunachal Pradesh, see the Sun rise before places further west, like Kutch.
I can give two pieces of evidence that the Earth really spins, like a Foucault pendulum and stars turning round the Pole Star.
I can say what scientists agree on about the Earth's spin, and what they still do not know.
I can link the spin to bigger ideas: days getting slowly longer, days on other planets, body clocks and why the night sky is dark.

terms.meaning: The time when our side of the Earth faces the Sun, so we get sunlight. People also say 'a day' for one whole spin of the Earth, which takes 24 hours.
terms.example: At 11 in the morning in Pune, it is day. The sky is bright and you can see without a lamp.
terms.art: A sunny Indian street at mid-morning with short shadows under people and a cow.

terms.meaning: The time when our side of the Earth faces away from the Sun. No sunlight reaches us, so it is dark.
terms.example: At 11 at night in Pune, it is dark. Street lights are on and the stars are out.
terms.art: The same street at night, with lit windows, street lamps and a few stars.

terms.meaning: The planet we live on. It is a huge rocky ball, and it floats in space.
terms.example: Every place you have ever been is on the Earth.
terms.art: The Earth as seen from space, with India visible under white clouds.

terms.meaning: The star at the centre of our solar system. It is a giant ball of very hot glowing gas. It gives us light and warmth.
terms.example: The Sun is so big that about a million Earths could fit inside it.
terms.art: A glowing Sun with a tiny Earth beside it, drawn to show the huge difference in size.

terms.meaning: A giant ball of hot gas that makes its own light. Our Sun is a star. The other stars are so far away that they look like tiny dots.
terms.example: Dhruva Tara, the Pole Star, is a star much bigger than our Sun. It looks small only because it is so far away.
terms.art: A night sky with tiny stars, and one zoomed-in star shown as a blazing ball.

terms.meaning: To turn round and round on the spot, like a top or a fan. Scientists say the Earth rotates.
terms.example: A lattu, a wooden spinning top, spins on its point. The Earth spins too, but much more slowly.
terms.art: A wooden lattu spinning on a floor, with a curved arrow around it.

terms.meaning: One whole spin. The Earth makes one rotation in about 24 hours. This rotation gives us day and night.
terms.example: From one sunrise to the next sunrise is about one rotation of the Earth.
terms.art: A ball with a dot on it shown in four positions, going all the way round.

terms.meaning: An imaginary line that a spinning thing turns around. The Earth's axis goes through the North Pole and the South Pole.
terms.example: Push a pencil through an orange and twirl it. The pencil is the orange's axis.
terms.art: An orange with a pencil pushed through it, top to bottom, being twirled.

terms.meaning: The two ends of the Earth's axis. They are the top and bottom points of the spinning Earth.
terms.example: The North Pole is in the middle of a frozen sea. The South Pole is on the icy land of Antarctica.
terms.art: A globe with the two poles marked by small flags, and the axis line between them.

terms.meaning: The moment the Sun first appears at the edge of the sky in the morning. Really, it is the moment our place on the Earth turns into the sunlight.
terms.example: The Sun always rises somewhere in the east.
terms.art: The Sun peeping over a line of hills, with the sky turning orange.

terms.meaning: The moment the Sun goes below the edge of the sky in the evening. Really, it is the moment our place turns away from the sunlight.
terms.example: The Sun always sets somewhere in the west.
terms.art: The Sun half hidden behind the sea at Mumbai's Marine Drive, the sky orange and pink.

terms.meaning: The middle of the day, when the Sun is at its highest in the sky. Shadows are shortest at noon.
terms.example: At noon your shadow is at its shortest. On a summer noon in India, it is only a small patch near your feet.
terms.art: A child at noon with a tiny shadow under their feet.

terms.meaning: The line far away where the land or the sea seems to meet the sky.
terms.example: At the beach, the horizon is the line where the sea meets the sky.
terms.art: A flat sea with a straight line where it meets the sky, an arrow pointing to the line.

terms.meaning: Two opposite directions. The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west. If you face the sunrise, west is behind you.
terms.example: Arunachal Pradesh is in the east of India. Gujarat is in the west.
terms.art: A child facing a sunrise, with the word E in front and W behind, shown with arrows only.

terms.meaning: The line on the Earth between the half in sunlight and the half in darkness. Places on this line are having sunrise or sunset. Scientists call it the terminator.
terms.example: On a ball lit by a torch, you can see a soft line where the light ends.
terms.art: A ball lit by a torch, with the soft edge between light and dark highlighted.

terms.meaning: When something seems to move, but really it is you who is moving. The Sun's movement across our sky is apparent.
terms.example: From a moving train, the trees seem to rush backwards. The trees are still. You are moving.
terms.art: A child at a train window, trees outside with motion lines going backwards.

terms.meaning: A dark shape made when something blocks the light. A shadow always falls on the side away from the light.
terms.example: In the morning, when the Sun is in the east, your shadow points west.
terms.art: A child in morning sunlight with a long shadow stretching away from the Sun.

terms.meaning: A weight hanging on a string or wire, swinging to and fro.
terms.example: A heavy nut tied to a string and swung gently is a pendulum. So is a swing in the park.
terms.art: A nut on a string swinging, with a dotted arc showing its path.

terms.meaning: A star that sits almost exactly above the North Pole. As the Earth spins, all the other stars seem to circle around it, but it hardly moves.
terms.example: From India, you find it in the northern sky, using the Saptarishi stars as pointers. The further south you live, the lower it sits.
terms.art: The Saptarishi stars with two pointer stars and a dotted line leading to Dhruva Tara.

terms.meaning: The soft light in the sky just before sunrise and just after sunset. The Sun is below the horizon, but the air above us still catches its light.
terms.example: After sunset, you can still see your way home for a while. That is twilight.
terms.art: A town just after sunset, the sky glowing deep blue and pink, lamps not yet needed.

terms.meaning: The path one thing takes as it goes round another in space. The Earth orbits the Sun once a year. That is a different movement from the spin.
terms.example: The Earth spins about 365 times while it goes once round the Sun.
terms.art: The Sun in the middle and the Earth on a big oval path around it, with a small spin arrow on the Earth.

terms.meaning: A timer inside living things that keeps track of day and night, even without a clock. It tells your body when to feel sleepy and when to wake.
terms.example: You often wake up at about the same time each day, even on holidays.
terms.art: A sleeping child with a tiny clock drawn inside their head, glowing softly.

explanations.concept: Day and night: half the Earth is always lit
explanations.definition: The Sun lights up the half of the Earth that faces it. There it is day. The other half is in the Earth's own shadow. There it is night.
explanations.description: The Sun shines all the time. It never switches off at night. But sunlight can only reach the side of the Earth that faces the Sun. The far side is dark, like the back of your head when you face a lamp. So at every moment, half of the Earth has day and half has night. When it is 9 at night in India, it is morning in parts of America. Their Sun is the very same Sun as ours.
examples: Hold an orange in front of a lamp in a dark room. The side facing the lamp is bright. The back is dark.
When you go to bed in Chennai, children in California are getting up for school.
From space, astronauts see the Earth as half bright and half dark, with cities glowing on the dark half.
explanations.art: The Earth seen from space, one half in sunlight and one half dark with city lights twinkling, the Sun far to the left.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what day and night are.

explanations.concept: The Earth spins, once in about 24 hours
explanations.definition: The Earth spins around an imaginary line called its axis. One whole spin takes about 24 hours. This spin is called rotation.
explanations.description: The Earth's axis goes through the North Pole and the South Pole. The Earth turns from west to east. If you looked down on the North Pole from space, you would see it turn anticlockwise. As it turns, every place is carried into the sunlight, across the middle of the day, and out into the dark again. That is one day and one night. The Earth is very big, so even one slow turn a day moves the ground very fast. In India, the ground moves at nearly 1,500 kilometres an hour. At the equator, the fattest part of the Earth, it moves at about 1,670 kilometres an hour.
examples: A dot drawn on a spinning ball goes into the torchlight, across it, and out again. That is like your town's day.
A ceiling fan spins around its middle rod. The Earth spins around its axis in the same way.
Places near the poles move slowly. Places near the equator move fastest, because they have the longest circle to go round.
explanations.art: A globe with a pencil-line axis through the poles, a curved arrow showing it turning west to east, and a small figure riding on India.
explanations.context: Why does every place get day and then night? This card explains the Earth's spin.

explanations.concept: The Sun only seems to move
explanations.definition: The Sun seems to rise in the east, cross the sky and set in the west. This is apparent movement. It is really the Earth turning under us.
explanations.description: Sit in a train as it pulls out of the station. The platform seems to slide backwards. The platform is still. You are the one moving. The sky works in the same way. The Earth turns from west to east. So we are carried towards the east, and the Sun seems to slide the other way, towards the west. In the morning our side of the Earth turns towards the Sun, and we call it sunrise. In the evening our side turns away, and we call it sunset. We still use the words sunrise and sunset. Scientists use them too. But nothing is rising or setting. Our ground is turning.
examples: From a moving bus, trees and poles seem to rush past backwards.
Spin slowly on a swivel chair. The whole room seems to turn around you.
The Moon and the stars also seem to rise in the east and set in the west, for the same reason.
explanations.art: Two panels: a child on a moving train with trees rushing backwards, and the same child standing on the turning Earth with the Sun seeming to slide across the sky.
explanations.context: We say the Sun rises and sets. This card explains what is really happening when the Sun crosses the sky.

explanations.concept: Aryabhata's boat: an idea from India, 499 CE
explanations.definition: Aryabhata, an Indian astronomer, wrote in 499 CE that the Earth turns, and that the stars only seem to move.
explanations.description: Aryabhata lived in Kusumapura, near today's Patna. When he was 23 years old, he finished a book called the Aryabhatiya. In it he gave an example. A man in a boat moving forward sees the trees on the bank moving backwards. In the same way, he said, the still stars seem to move west. So the Earth must be turning. Most astronomers of his time disagreed. Later Indian astronomers, including Brahmagupta, argued against him. Aryabhata had no way to prove it. About a thousand years later, Copernicus in Poland also wrote that the Earth spins, in 1543. Today we know Aryabhata was right.
examples: From a boat on the Ganga, the ghats seem to glide past, though the boat is the thing that moves.
Greek thinkers also had this idea. Heraclides of Pontus said the Earth turns, about 2,300 years ago.
explanations.art: A man in a wooden boat on a wide river at night, the trees on the bank drawn with backward motion lines, stars above.
explanations.context: Who first said that the Earth spins? This card is about an Indian astronomer who said it about 1,500 years ago.

explanations.concept: Why we do not feel the Earth spin
explanations.definition: We do not feel the spin because it is smooth and steady, and everything around us moves with us.
explanations.description: You only feel movement when it changes: a speed-up, a slow-down, a bump or a sharp turn. In a smooth train, with your eyes shut, you can hardly tell that you are moving. The Earth's spin is smoother than any train. It never brakes and never bumps. The ground, the air, the birds and you all move together. So when you jump, you land in the same place. The ground does not slide away under you, because you were already moving with it. Galileo, an Italian scientist, explained this in 1632. He said a stone dropped from the top of a ship's mast lands at the foot of the mast, even while the ship sails.
examples: Toss a ball straight up in a smoothly moving train. It falls back into your hand.
In an aeroplane flying smoothly, you can pour water into a cup without spilling.
Clouds and birds are not left behind. The air moves with the Earth.
explanations.art: A child on a smooth train tossing a ball straight up and catching it, the countryside blurred outside.
explanations.context: If the ground is moving so fast, why can't we feel it? This card explains.

explanations.concept: How we know the Earth really spins
explanations.definition: Several kinds of evidence show that it is the Earth that spins, not the sky that turns. One famous piece is the Foucault pendulum.
explanations.description: In 1851, a French scientist, Léon Foucault, hung a heavy ball on a 67-metre wire in the Panthéon, a great hall in Paris. A swinging pendulum keeps swinging in the same direction unless something pushes it sideways. But as the hours went by, the swing seemed to turn slowly around the floor. Nothing was pushing it. The floor, and the whole Earth, was turning under it. In Paris, the swing goes all the way round in about 32 hours. In Delhi it takes about 50 hours. India's new Parliament building, opened in 2023, has a Foucault pendulum too. There is more evidence. All the stars wheel around the Pole Star once a day. Big storms like cyclones spin one way north of the equator and the other way south of it. And cameras on satellites have filmed the Earth turning.
examples: A long-exposure photo pointed at the Pole Star shows the stars as curved streaks around it.
Cyclones over the Bay of Bengal always spin anticlockwise. In Australia, they spin clockwise.
Satellites photograph the day-night line sliding across the Earth.
explanations.art: A tall hall with a heavy brass ball swinging on a long wire over a circle of little pegs, some knocked over, a curved arrow on the floor.
explanations.context: How can we be sure the Earth spins, when we cannot feel it? This card gives the evidence.

show.art: A pendulum swinging along a chalk line drawn on a round stool.
show.caption: The pendulum swings along the line.

show.art: The same pendulum swinging in the same direction, but the stool and its chalk line have turned a quarter turn underneath.
show.caption: The stool turns. The swing does not.

explanations.definition: The Earth turns from west to east, so places in the east of India turn into the sunlight first. Sunrise sweeps across the country from east to west.
explanations.description: Dong, a village in Arunachal Pradesh, is one of the first places in India to see the sunrise. In June, about two hours later, the Sun rises in the far west of Kutch, in Gujarat. Between them, sunrise reaches Kolkata, then Nagpur, then Mumbai. But all of India uses one clock time, called Indian Standard Time. It is set by the Sun over a line passing near Mirzapur, in Uttar Pradesh, close to the middle of the country. So in Arunachal, the clock says it is early when the Sun is already up. In Gujarat, the clock says it is late when the Sun has only just risen. Tea gardens in Assam have long used their own clock, called tea garden time, one hour ahead of the rest of India.
examples: On a summer morning, the Sun can rise in Dong before 4:30, by the clock.
In Bhuj, in Kutch, summer sunrise comes at about 6 o'clock.
In Guwahati in June, the Sun is up by about 4:30 by the clock, long before shops and offices open.
explanations.art: A map of India with a soft golden line of sunrise sweeping from Arunachal Pradesh in the east towards Gujarat in the west, small suns marking Dong, Kolkata, Mumbai and Bhuj.
explanations.context: Does the Sun rise at the same time all over India? This card shows that it does not, and why.

chart.title: About when the Sun rises on a day in June, by Indian clock time (rounded)
chart.note: Times are rounded and change a little through the year. Delhi comes before Mumbai for two reasons. It is further east, and in June places further north get an earlier sunrise.

explanations.concept: What a day really is: two kinds of day
explanations.definition: One spin measured against the far stars takes about 23 hours and 56 minutes. One day from noon to noon takes 24 hours. Our clocks use the 24-hour day.
explanations.description: While the Earth spins, it is also travelling on its long path around the Sun. So after one full spin, the Sun is no longer in quite the same place in our sky. The Earth has to turn about 4 minutes more to bring the Sun back to the top of the sky. So a star comes back to the same place 4 minutes earlier each night. Over a year, that adds up. That is why the night sky in December shows different stars from the night sky in June.
examples: If you see a bright star above a rooftop at 9 tonight, it will be there at about 8:56 tomorrow.
Orion, the hunter, is easy to see on winter evenings in India, but not on summer evenings.
explanations.art: The Earth shown twice on its curved path round the Sun, a little further along the second time, with a small extra turn arrow.
explanations.context: Is a day exactly one spin of the Earth? This card shows that there are two kinds of day, 4 minutes apart.

explanations.concept: Why the Earth spins at all
explanations.description: Scientists think the Earth got its spin when it was born, about 4.5 billion years ago. The Sun and planets formed from a huge, slowly swirling cloud of gas and dust. As the cloud squashed together, it spun faster, the way a spinning dancer turns faster when she pulls her arms in. The lumps that became the Earth were spinning too. Then many think a planet about the size of Mars crashed into the young Earth. The bits thrown out became the Moon. That crash probably changed the Earth's spin as well. In space, there is almost nothing to rub against, so a spinning thing keeps spinning. That is why the Earth is still turning today. The broad story is widely accepted. The details, like how fast the young Earth spun, are still being worked out.
examples: Spin on a swivel chair with your arms out, then pull them in. You speed up.
A spinning top slows down because its point rubs the floor. The Earth has no floor to rub.

perspectives.explanation: The spin came from the swirling cloud the solar system formed from, and was changed by big crashes, like the one that made the Moon.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study the early Earth
perspectives.explanation: How long the very first days were is not known. Some estimates say just a few hours. Rocks and computer models give different answers.

explanations.art: A swirling disc of gas and dust around a young glowing Sun, with lumps clumping together, and one small young Earth spinning.
explanations.context: Why is the Earth spinning in the first place? This card gives scientists' best ideas, which are not all settled.

explanations.definition: The Earth's spin is very slowly slowing down. So each day is a tiny bit longer than days long ago.
explanations.description: The Moon's gravity pulls the oceans into a bulge, which makes the tides. As the Earth turns, the sea rubs against the sea floor. This friction acts like a gentle brake on the Earth's spin. A day gets about 2 thousandths of a second longer every 100 years. That is far too little to notice in a lifetime. But over millions of years it adds up. In 1963, John Wells, an American scientist, counted daily growth lines on fossil corals 400 million years old. He found that a year then had about 400 days, so each day was only about 22 hours long. In 2020, a team led by Niels de Winter studied a fossil shell from the time of the dinosaurs. They found that a day then was about half an hour shorter than ours.
examples: A coral adds a thin layer each day, like a diary written in stone.
The Moon is also slowly moving away from us, by about 4 centimetres a year. Mirrors left on the Moon by astronauts let scientists measure this with lasers.
explanations.art: A fossil coral cut open to show many thin growth lines, with a magnifying glass over them, and a tiny clock showing 22 hours.
explanations.context: Has a day always been 24 hours long? This card shows that days were once shorter, and how we know.

chart.title: How long one day was, long ago (rounded, from fossil corals and shells)
chart.note: These are scientists' best estimates. Each one has some uncertainty.

explanations.definition: Every planet spins at its own speed, so a day lasts a different time on each planet.
explanations.description: Jupiter is the biggest planet, yet it spins fastest. Its day is only about 10 hours long. A day on Mars is a little longer than ours, about 24 hours and 40 minutes. Venus spins very slowly, and backwards. On Venus the Sun rises in the west. One spin of Venus takes 243 of our days. Our Moon turns once each time it goes round the Earth. That is why we always see the same face of the Moon. On the Moon, from one sunrise to the next takes about 29 and a half of our days.
examples: On Jupiter you could see two sunrises in one of our days, if you could see through its thick clouds.
Scientists working with the rovers on Mars once lived on Mars time, so their clock slid later by about 40 minutes every day.
explanations.art: Four little planets in a row, Jupiter, Earth, Mars and Venus, each with a small clock face and a spin arrow, Venus's arrow going the other way.
explanations.context: Is a day the same length on every planet? This card compares the days on other worlds.

chart.title: How long a sunrise-to-sunrise day lasts, in our hours (rounded)
chart.note: Venus is left out because its day is so long it would not fit. It lasts about 117 of our days, which is about 2,800 hours.

explanations.concept: Midnight Sun and long nights near the poles
explanations.definition: Near the North and South Poles, there are weeks when the Sun never sets, and weeks when it never rises.
explanations.description: The Earth's axis is tilted, like a top leaning a little to one side. For part of the year, the North Pole leans towards the Sun. Then places near it stay in sunlight all the way round the spin, for weeks on end. The Sun just circles around the sky, low down, all day and all night. People call this the midnight Sun. Half a year later, the North Pole leans away, and the Sun does not rise for weeks. India has a research station called Himadri, in Svalbard, far up in the Arctic. Indian scientists there work under the midnight Sun in summer. Why the tilt also gives us seasons is the subject of another unit.
examples: In Svalbard, the Sun does not set from about the middle of April to late August.
At India's Antarctic stations, Maitri and Bharati, scientists have long dark weeks in the southern winter.
explanations.art: A snowy Arctic landscape with a small research hut, and a dotted line showing the Sun circling low around the sky without ever touching the horizon.
explanations.context: Does every place on Earth get a day and a night every 24 hours? This card is about places where they do not.

explanations.concept: Twilight, and the Sun you see after it has set
explanations.definition: After sunset, the air above us still catches sunlight, so the sky stays bright for a while. This is twilight. The air also bends sunlight a little. So we still see the Sun for about 2 minutes after it has really gone below the horizon.
explanations.description: Air scatters sunlight, sending it off in all directions, and this lights up the whole sky. That is why the daytime sky is bright, and not black like space. After sunset, high air is still in sunlight, so it glows for a while. Air also bends light a little, like water bends a straw in a glass. Near the horizon, this bending lifts the picture of the Sun. So at sunset, the Sun you see touching the horizon is already just below it. Look east just after sunset and you may see a dark blue band low in the sky, with a pink band above it. The dark band is the shadow of the Earth itself, falling on the air.
examples: On the Moon there is no air, so the sky is black even in the day, and there is no twilight.
Astronauts on the International Space Station go round the Earth so fast that they see about 16 sunrises a day.
explanations.art: A view east just after sunset: a dark blue band of the Earth's shadow along the horizon, a soft pink band above it, and a child pointing.
explanations.context: Why doesn't it get dark the moment the Sun sets? This card explains twilight.

explanations.concept: Why the night sky is dark
explanations.definition: The night sky is dark because the universe as we know it began about 13.8 billion years ago. Light from the most distant stars has not had time to reach us. And light from very far away is stretched so much that our eyes cannot see it.
explanations.description: This sounds like a silly question, but it puzzled great scientists. There are so many stars that, wherever you look, your eye should end up on a star. So why isn't the whole night sky as bright as the Sun? Johannes Kepler wondered about this in 1610. Heinrich Olbers, a German doctor and astronomer, wrote about it in 1823. Then in 1848, Edgar Allan Poe, a writer of stories and poems, made a clever guess. Maybe light from the most distant stars has not reached us yet. Today scientists agree he was largely right. The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago, so light has only had that long to travel. Also, space is stretching, which stretches far-away light until it is too dim and too red to see.
examples: Stand in a big forest. Wherever you look, you see a tree trunk. A night sky full of stars should be like that, but it is not.
explanations.art: A child on a rooftop looking at a dark sky full of stars, with a thought bubble showing a sky packed with stars and glowing white.
explanations.context: Night is dark because we face away from the Sun. But space has billions of other suns. This card asks why they do not light up the night.

explanations.description: A Foucault pendulum keeps its swing still compared with the far-away stars and galaxies, while the Earth turns underneath. Water in a spinning bucket climbs up the sides. In both cases, the spin seems to be measured against the whole distant universe. But why should the far stars decide what counts as spinning? Physicists have argued about this for more than 300 years.
examples: Stir water fast in a steel bowl, then stop stirring. While the water spins, it climbs up the sides and dips in the middle.
In a spinning room with no windows, a pendulum would still show the spin.

perspectives.who: Isaac Newton, an English scientist, in 1687
perspectives.explanation: Space itself is a fixed stage. Spinning means turning compared with that stage, even if nothing else existed.

perspectives.who: Ernst Mach, an Austrian scientist, in 1883
perspectives.explanation: Spinning only means something compared with all the matter in the universe. If the whole universe were empty, spinning might mean nothing. His idea inspired Albert Einstein.

Einstein's theory of gravity says the spinning Earth very slightly drags space around with it. A satellite called Gravity Probe B measured this tiny effect in 2011. But whether Mach was right is still argued.

explanations.art: A small Earth spinning inside a giant sphere of faint galaxies, with a pendulum on the Earth keeping its swing lined up with the galaxies.
explanations.context: We say the Earth spins. This card asks a deeper question: spinning compared with what?

explanations.concept: Living things keep time with the spin
explanations.definition: Plants, animals and people have body clocks inside them. Body clocks follow a rhythm of about 24 hours, matching the Earth's spin.
explanations.description: In 1729, a French astronomer, Jean-Jacques d'Ortous de Mairan, put a touch-me-not plant in a dark cupboard. Its leaves still opened in the day and folded at night, without any sunlight. So the plant had its own clock. In 1962, a young French cave explorer, Michel Siffre, lived alone in a cave for about two months, with no clock and no daylight. He kept a rhythm of waking and sleeping. But it drifted, and when he came out he thought it was about 25 days earlier than it really was. In 2017, three American scientists won the Nobel Prize for finding the genes that work the clock, in fruit flies. Almost every cell in our body has a clock like that. Morning light reaching our eyes resets the main clock, in the brain, every day.
examples: Owls, bats and many moths are active at night. Scientists call them nocturnal.
Long flights across the world give people jet lag. Their body clock is still on home time.
explanations.art: A touch-me-not plant inside a dark cupboard with its leaves open, and a little clock drawn faintly in its stem.
explanations.context: The Earth has spun every day for billions of years. This card shows how living things have a clock that matches it.

explanations.definition: Daylight is light from the Sun. The Sun makes it deep inside, where hydrogen is squeezed into helium and gives out huge amounts of energy.
explanations.description: In 1925, a young astronomer, Cecilia Payne, showed that the Sun and the stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium. Many senior astronomers did not believe her at first. Later, they agreed she was right. Deep in the Sun's centre, hydrogen is squeezed so hard that it joins together into helium. This gives out the energy that makes sunlight. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to cross space and reach your face. But scientists estimate that its energy spent many thousands of years working its way out from the Sun's centre first. So the energy in the morning light on your face began its journey out of the Sun's centre long before the first towns were built.
examples: When you see the Sun, you see it as it was about 8 minutes ago.
Plants catch this sunlight and make food from it, and so do we, when we eat the plants.
explanations.art: A cutaway of the Sun with a bright core, a wiggly path of light working its way out, then a straight beam crossing space to a child's face at sunrise.
explanations.context: Day happens when sunlight reaches us. This card follows that light back to where it was made.

agreed.text: Day and night happen because the Earth spins. At any moment, half of the Earth faces the Sun and has day.
agreed.evidence: Photos from satellites show the Earth half lit and half dark, with the day-night line moving across it. A ball and a torch show the same thing at home.

agreed.text: The Earth spins once in about 24 hours, from west to east.
agreed.evidence: Every place on Earth gets one sunrise and one sunset in about 24 hours, except near the poles. The Sun, Moon and stars all seem to move from east to west.

agreed.text: The Sun's movement across our sky is only apparent. The Sun is not going round the Earth each day.
agreed.evidence: Foucault's pendulum, first shown in Paris in 1851, turns its swing as the floor turns. Stars trace circles around the Pole Star. Spacecraft have filmed the Earth turning.

agreed.text: Places further east see the Sun rise earlier.
agreed.evidence: Sunrise times printed in newspapers show it. In June, the Sun rises in Dong, in Arunachal Pradesh, about two hours before it rises in Bhuj, in Kutch.

agreed.text: The Earth's spin is very slowly slowing down, so days are getting longer.
agreed.evidence: Records of ancient eclipses, daily growth lines in fossil corals and shells, and laser measurements of the Moon all agree. A day gets about 2 thousandths of a second longer every 100 years.

challenging.claim: The Earth stands still at the centre, and the Sun goes round it every day.
challenging.who: Most people in most places for thousands of years, and Ptolemy, a Greek astronomer in Egypt, about 1,900 years ago
challenging.for: It is exactly what we see. The ground feels still. The Sun really does seem to travel across the sky.
challenging.against: Seeming to move is not the same as moving. A Foucault pendulum's swing turns as the Earth turns under it. Stars wheel around the Pole Star. Photos from space show the Earth spinning. The Sun stays put, and we turn.
challenging.context: This card is about the oldest idea of all about day and night, and why scientists gave it up.

challenging.claim: If the Earth were spinning, birds and clouds would be left behind, and we would be thrown off.
challenging.who: Ptolemy, in his book the Almagest, and many people since
challenging.for: The ground would be moving very fast. Fast spinning things, like a merry-go-round, can throw you off.
challenging.against: The air, the birds and the clouds all move along with the Earth, just as the air inside a train moves with the train. The Earth spins once a day, which is very gentle compared with a merry-go-round. Gravity holds us on far more strongly than the spin could throw us off.
challenging.context: This card is about an old reason people gave for why the Earth could not be spinning.

challenging.claim: Copernicus, in Poland, was the first to say that the Earth spins.
challenging.for: Copernicus wrote it in his famous book of 1543, and it changed science in Europe.
challenging.against: Aryabhata wrote it in India in 499 CE, more than a thousand years earlier, with his example of a man in a moving boat. Heraclides of Pontus said it in Greece even earlier. Their ideas were argued against and often forgotten.
challenging.context: This card is about who should get the credit for the idea that the Earth spins.

challenging.claim: At night, the Sun goes behind the mountains, or sinks into the sea, or goes to sleep.
challenging.who: Many old stories around the world, and many young children
challenging.for: The Sun does seem to sink behind the hills or into the sea at sunset.
challenging.against: When the Sun sets for us, it is rising for someone else. People phoning or video-calling across the world see this every day. The Sun never goes anywhere. Our side of the Earth turns away from it.
challenging.context: This card is about ideas of where the Sun goes at night.

challenging.claim: At noon, the Sun is straight overhead everywhere, so there is no shadow.
challenging.for: At noon the Sun is at its highest, and shadows are shortest.
challenging.against: In most of the world, the Sun is never exactly overhead, so there is always some shadow at noon. In places between the equator and the Tropic of Cancer, like Bengaluru and Chennai, there are just two days each year with no noon shadow. People in India call them Zero Shadow Days.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the noon Sun is always straight above our heads.

challenging.claim: Water going down a sink swirls one way in India and the other way in Australia, because the Earth spins.
challenging.who: A popular claim, often shown to tourists near the equator
challenging.for: The Earth's spin really does make huge storms, like cyclones, turn one way north of the equator and the other way south of it.
challenging.against: A sink is far too small for the spin to matter. The shape of the sink and the way the water was poured decide how it swirls. In careful tests with very still water in a big round tank, scientists have seen the spin's effect, but never in an ordinary sink.
challenging.context: The Earth's spin makes big storms turn. This card asks whether it also turns the water in your sink.

big_questions.q: You are moving at nearly 1,500 kilometres an hour right now, and you cannot feel it. What else might be true that you cannot feel?
big_questions.hint: Think of the air pressing on you, the blood moving in you, and the light from stars arriving in your eyes.

big_questions.q: Somewhere on the Earth, it is always sunrise. Is there ever a moment when the whole world is asleep?
big_questions.hint: Spin a ball under a torch slowly. Is there ever a moment with no place on the day-night line?

big_questions.q: If you lived on the Moon, where one day lasts about a month, how would you know when to sleep?
big_questions.hint: Think about body clocks, and the astronauts who see 16 sunrises a day.

big_questions.q: We still say 'the Sun rises', though we know the Earth turns. Are there other things we say that are not really true?
big_questions.hint: Think of 'the Moon follows our car', or 'a shooting star'. What is really happening?

big_questions.q: Aryabhata believed the Earth turns, but he could not prove it. Most people around him disagreed. When is it right to believe something before it is proved?
big_questions.hint: What reasons did he have? Was the boat example a proof, or a good argument?

big_questions.q: Why does a spinning thing keep spinning? What would it take to stop the Earth?
big_questions.hint: A top stops because its point rubs the floor. What does the Earth have to rub against?

big_questions.q: The night is when owls, bats, moths and many frogs live their busiest lives. When we light up the night, whose world are we changing?
big_questions.hint: Look at the insects around a street lamp tonight.

big_questions.q: If days keep getting longer, will people one day have 25-hour days? What would you do with the extra hour?
big_questions.hint: Days grow about 2 thousandths of a second longer every 100 years. How long would it take to add a whole hour?

big_questions.q: Night workers, like nurses, bakers and drivers, keep the world going while we sleep. Do we notice them?
big_questions.hint: Who was awake last night so that your milk, bread or medicine was ready this morning?

big_questions.q: The Sun you see at sunset is already just below the horizon, and its light left the Sun 8 minutes ago. Do we ever see things exactly as they are, right now?
big_questions.hint: Light takes time to travel. So does sound. What about the stars?

big_questions.q: A Foucault pendulum keeps its swing lined up with the far-away stars, not with the turning floor. Why should the far stars decide what counts as spinning?
big_questions.hint: Scientists still argue about this. The stars are very far away. What could link them to a pendulum in a hall?

story.title: The Rooster Who Raised the Sun
story.note: Dong is a real village in Arunachal Pradesh, one of the first places in India to see the sunrise. In June the Sun rises there about two hours before it rises in Bhuj, in Kutch. Raja, Mili, her family and their journey are made up. The idea of a rooster who thinks his crowing raises the Sun is old, for example in Edmond Rostand's French play Chantecler (1910). This story is new.
text: I am Raja, and I am the rooster of Dong. Dong is a small village high in the hills of Arunachal Pradesh, where two rivers meet. Every child in India should know about Dong, because Dong is where the Sun comes up. I know this for certain. I am the one who brings it up.

Every morning, while the whole of India is still asleep, I wake in the dark. I climb onto the woodpile, fill my chest with cold mountain air, and crow. Ko-ko-ro-koooo! The darkness grows thin and grey. I crow again. A line of gold appears behind the eastern hills. One more crow, my loudest, and up comes the Sun. Every single morning. I have never once failed.

My girl is called Mili. She is nine, and she feeds me rice from her own bowl. So when Mili's mother got a teaching job far away in Bhuj, in Kutch, at the other end of India, Mili refused to go without me. 'Raja comes too,' she said, 'or I stay with Grandmother.' So I came, in a bamboo basket with a cloth over the top.

It was a long journey. A jeep took us down the hills. Then we took trains for four days and four nights. On the first morning, on the train, I woke at my usual time. I crowed. People in the compartment groaned and pulled their sheets over their heads. And the Sun did not come up.

I crowed again. Nothing. The sky stayed black. I crowed until a man in the top berth threw a pillow at my basket. It was a long, long time before the window turned grey, and then gold. Mili looked at her mother's watch and frowned.

Every morning on that train, the dark after my crow lasted a little longer. It was as if the Sun were growing deaf. Or, I thought, with a cold feeling in my feathers, as if my crow were growing weak. Perhaps my power belonged to the hills of Dong. Perhaps, far from home, I was just an ordinary bird.

On our first morning in Bhuj, I woke at my usual time and climbed onto the wall of our new courtyard. The air was warm and smelled of dust and salt. I crowed my best crow. The sky stayed as black as a cooking pot.

I crowed for half an hour. A dog barked at me. A neighbour shouted something in Kutchi that I did not understand, and a chappal flew over the wall. I crowed for an hour. My voice cracked. Still no Sun. At last, I gave up. I sat on the wall with my head down. My power was gone. India would have no more mornings, and it was my fault.

And then, while I sat there silent, the sky turned grey. Then pink. Then gold. And the Sun came up over the flat land of Kutch, big and round, as if nothing were wrong at all. I had not made a single sound.

I did not eat my rice that day. Mili noticed. In the evening, she carried me up onto the flat roof to watch the sunset. The Sun hung low and orange over the salty plain. Then Mili's phone buzzed. It was Grandmother, calling from Dong.
'Is it dark there yet?' Mili asked.

'Dark?' said Grandmother. 'Child, the Sun set here an hour and a half ago. The stars are out. I am about to go to bed.' She turned her phone to show us. Her screen was black, with a few small stars. Mili looked at Grandmother's dark screen. Then she looked at our Sun, still sitting there, orange, over Kutch.

Mili ran downstairs. She came back with a mausambi from the kitchen, a pen and her father's torch. On one side of the mausambi she drew a dot and wrote 'Dong'. A little way round, she drew another dot and wrote 'Bhuj'. She pushed a pencil through the fruit, from top to bottom, and shone the torch at it. 'Look, Raja,' she said. 'This is the Earth. The torch is the Sun.'

She turned the mausambi slowly on its pencil. The dot that said Dong came round into the torchlight first. Bhuj was still in the dark. She kept turning. Only later did Bhuj come round into the light too. 'The Sun doesn't come up,' Mili whispered. 'We go round to meet it. Dong turns into the light first. Bhuj turns into it two hours later. Your crow was right on time, Raja. You were just still on Dong time.'

I looked at the mausambi turning in the torchlight. Then I looked at the real Sun. It was sitting quite still. It had always been sitting still. It was the roof under my feet that was moving. The whole of Kutch, with its salt and dust and dogs, was tipping slowly backwards, away from the light. I could almost feel it, a slow, enormous lean, like a boat on a calm river.
The Sun had never been listening to me. All those years in Dong, my hill had simply been the first to turn into the light. I was not the one who raised the Sun. I was the first one who saw it.

That night, I thought about the line of light. It swept across India every morning, like a lamp carried slowly through a house. First it touched Dong, where Grandmother's rooster would be crowing. Then the tea gardens of Assam. Then Kolkata, then Delhi, then Mumbai, and at last, Bhuj. Then it would go on, across the sea, to Arabia and Africa, and on and on around the whole turning world. Somewhere along that line, a rooster was always crowing. Somewhere, it was always morning.

The next day, I woke at my Dong time. I waited in the dark, quietly, for about two hours. When the first grey came, I climbed onto the wall and crowed, softly at first, then loud. Not to call the Sun. Just to tell Bhuj that it had turned round into the morning once again.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the rooster thinks the Sun comes to him. The turn comes when the Sun rises without his crow, and Grandmother's sky in Dong is dark while Bhuj still has sunset. The mausambi on a pencil shows why. The Earth turns from west to east, so Dong turns into the sunlight about two hours before Bhuj. Nothing rises. The ground turns. The rooster's crow was not wrong, only still on Dong time, the way our body clocks keep home time after a long journey. The story also gently asks what happens when we think we are the centre that everything moves around.
ask: Why did Raja think he made the Sun rise?
On the train, why did the dark after Raja's crow last a little longer every morning?
When it was sunset in Bhuj, why was it already night for Grandmother in Dong?
What did Mili's mausambi, pencil and torch show? Can you do it too?
Raja learned he was 'the first one who saw it', not 'the one who raised it'. Have you ever thought something happened because of you, and then found out it did not?
