games.title: Who Sees the Sun First?
games.players: 2 to 4 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: This is a card game about sunrise travelling around the spinning Earth. Players race to put places in the order they turn into the sunlight, from east to west.

printables.title: 20 cards to cut out: 15 place cards, each with a small map dot, and 5 SPIN CARDS
items: Dong, Arunachal Pradesh (far east of India)
Bhuj, Kutch, Gujarat (far west of India)
Dubai, United Arab Emirates (west of India)
SPIN CARD: spin the ball one quarter turn. Which places are now in the light?
SPIN CARD: it is noon in Delhi. Name one place on the cards where it is night.
SPIN CARD: it is sunset in Kolkata. Is it still day in Mumbai?
SPIN CARD: a rooster in Dong crows at sunrise. Who crows next, Kolkata or Mumbai?
SPIN CARD: it is midnight in India. Is anyone having sunrise?

rules: Cut out the cards. Lay the sunrise line strip on the floor. Have a ball and a torch ready.
Shuffle the place cards and deal 3 to each player. Put the rest face down in a pile.
On your turn, put one of your place cards on the sunrise line. It must be in the right order, east first. Then take a new card from the pile.
If someone thinks it is in the wrong place, check on a map or a globe. A right card wins one paper sun. A wrong card goes back in the pile.
If you get a SPIN CARD, read it out. Everyone answers it together using the ball and the torch. The first right answer wins two suns.
When the pile runs out, the player with the most suns wins.

setup.art: A long paper strip on the floor with a small sun at one end, and a pile of picture cards of places beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the sunrise line. Deal 3 place cards each.

setup.art: A child placing a card that shows Kolkata between cards showing Dong and Mumbai on the strip.
setup.caption: 2. Put a card on the line, in the right order.

setup.art: A ball with sticker dots, lit by a torch, and a child turning it to check a SPIN CARD.
setup.caption: 3. For a SPIN CARD, check with the ball and the torch.

flow.do: 1. Lay the sunrise line strip on the floor. If you know which way is east, put the 'first' end on that side. 2. Shuffle the place cards. Deal 3 to each player. 3. Put a ball and a torch nearby.
flow.say: The Earth spins from west to east. So places in the east turn into the sunlight first. Let's put places in the order they see sunrise.
flow.kid: Lay out the sunrise line. Deal 3 cards each. Places in the east see the Sun first. Let's put them in order.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Sees the Sun First?. It is a card game about sunrise travelling across the spinning Earth.

flow.do: Practise with two cards: Dong and Bhuj. Ask which goes first on the line.
flow.say: Here are Dong, in Arunachal Pradesh, and Bhuj, in Kutch. Which one sees the Sun first?
flow.kid: Practice round. Dong is in the far east of India. Bhuj is in the far west. Who sees the Sun first?

check.q: Who sees the sunrise first, Dong in the east or Bhuj in the west?
check.why: The Earth turns from west to east. So the eastern places turn into the sunlight first. Dong sees the Sun about two hours before Bhuj. Picking 'Bhuj' often means thinking the Sun travels to us from the west. Picking 'the same moment' usually comes from India having one clock time. The clock is the same, but the sunrise is not.

flow.do: 1. Take turns placing cards on the line. 2. Check any argued card on a map or globe. 3. Give one paper sun for each right card.
flow.say: Put your card down and tell us why it goes there. Is it east or west of its neighbour?
flow.kid: Your turn. Put a card on the line. Say why it goes there. Is it more east, or more west?
flow.parent: A rough order from east to west is this. Tokyo, Singapore, Dong, Guwahati, Dhaka, Kolkata, Bhubaneswar, Chennai, Delhi, Mumbai, Bhuj, Dubai, Nairobi, London, New York. Singapore and Tokyo are east of India, so they see the Sun before us. How far north or south a place is also changes sunrise a little. In June, Dong sees the Sun even before Singapore, because Dong is further north. So close calls are fine. Focus on east and west. The noon Sun follows the east-to-west order exactly.

flow.do: When someone draws a SPIN CARD, stop. Use the ball and the torch to find the answer together.
flow.say: Let's check it on our Earth ball. Shine the torch from one side, and turn the ball slowly from west to east.
flow.kid: A SPIN CARD! Guess first. Then turn the ball under the torch to check.

ask.q: It is midnight in India. Is anyone having sunrise?
good: Yes. Places about a quarter of the way round the world to the east, like islands in the Pacific Ocean, are just turning into the light.
Yes. Somewhere is always on the day-night line.

flow.think: Is there ever a moment when no place on Earth is having sunrise?

flow.do: 1. Count the suns to find the winner. 2. Read the whole line out loud, from first sunrise to last.
flow.say: Let's read our line from east to west. This is the order the morning arrives in.
flow.kid: Count your suns. Who won? Now read the line from east to west. That is how the morning travels.
flow.think: When New York has its sunrise, what time of day is it for you?

games.title: Turn, Earth, Turn!
games.players: 3 or more players: one is the Sun, the others are the Earth
games.context: This is a moving game. Children hold hands in a ring and turn slowly, acting as the spinning Earth. Whoever faces the Sun acts out a day job or a day animal. Whoever faces away acts out a night one.

printables.title: 16 action cards
items: DAY: a farmer ploughing a field
DAY: a sunbird sipping from a flower
DAY: a lotus flower opening in the morning
DAY: a squirrel running along a wall
DAY: drying clothes on a line
NIGHT: a baker making bread for morning
NIGHT: a nurse looking after patients
NIGHT: a gecko catching insects by a lamp
NIGHT: an astronomer looking through a telescope

printables.title: A big yellow Sun sign to hold

rules: One player holds the yellow SUN sign and stands still at one side. The Sun never moves.
Everyone else holds hands in a small ring in the middle, facing outwards. The ring is the Earth.
The ring walks slowly round, anticlockwise when seen from above, one step at a time.

When the Sun calls 'Freeze!', everyone stops. Players facing the Sun take a DAY card and act it. Players facing away take a NIGHT card and act it. A player at the side who is turning towards the Sun says 'Sunrise!'. One turning away says 'Sunset!'.
Then swap so a new player is the Sun. Keep a count of the turns on the spin counter.

setup.art: A child holding a big yellow SUN sign at one side of a room, standing still.
setup.caption: 1. One player is the Sun, and stands still.

setup.art: Four children holding hands in a ring facing outwards, walking slowly round, arrows showing the turn.
setup.caption: 2. The others hold hands in a ring, facing out, and turn slowly.

setup.art: The ring frozen, with the children facing the Sun acting a farmer and a butterfly, and those facing away acting an owl and a sleeping person.
setup.caption: 3. On 'Freeze!', act a day card or a night card.

flow.do: 1. Choose one player to be the Sun. Give them the yellow sign. 2. The others hold hands in a ring, facing outwards. 3. Shuffle the DAY and NIGHT cards into two piles.
flow.say: The Sun stands still. We are the Earth. We will turn slowly, and see who gets day and who gets night.
flow.kid: One person is the Sun, and stands still. Everyone else makes a ring, facing out. You are the Earth!
flow.context: This is the first step of Turn, Earth, Turn!. In this game, children act as the spinning Earth and find out who has day and who has night.

flow.do: 1. The ring turns slowly. 2. The Sun calls 'Freeze!' every few steps. 3. Players facing the Sun act a DAY card. Players facing away act a NIGHT card. 4. Players at the edges call 'Sunrise!' or 'Sunset!'.
flow.say: Turn slowly. Freeze! Who can see the Sun? You have day. Who has their back to it? You have night.
flow.kid: Turn slowly. When the Sun says freeze, stop. Can you see the Sun? Act a day card. Can't see it? Act a night card.
flow.parent: Turn anticlockwise, seen from above. A child on the edge who is just turning towards the Sun is at sunrise. One just turning away is at sunset. Notice that the Sun player never moves. Every change comes from the turning ring.

check.q: In the game, why did some players have night?
options: Their backs were turned to the Sun
The Sun moved away from them
check.why: The Sun player stayed in the same place the whole time. Night came to the players whose side of the ring faced away from it. That is just how night happens on the real Earth. Picking 'the Sun moved' is the old idea that the Sun goes round us. Picking 'switched off' mixes up night with a light being turned off. The Sun shines all the time.

flow.do: Let the ring turn once all the way round. Count how many 'Sunrise!' calls each player makes.
flow.say: Let's go all the way round once. How many sunrises did each of you get?
flow.kid: Go all the way round once. How many sunrises did you get?

ask.q: One full turn of the ring gave each of you how many sunrises? What is that like on the real Earth?
good: One. One full spin of the Earth gives one day and one night.
One sunrise each turn, and one turn of the Earth takes about 24 hours.

flow.do: Ask the bonus question. For a harder version, the ring keeps turning and also walks slowly in a big circle around the Sun player.
flow.say: The real Earth also travels slowly round the Sun once a year. It spins about 365 times on that journey. Shall we try turning and travelling at once?
flow.kid: Bonus! The Earth also goes round the Sun. It spins 365 times on the way. Can you turn and travel at once?
flow.think: If the ring stopped turning, what would happen to the players on the night side?

items.p: Why do we have day and night?
opts: The Sun goes round the Earth every day
The Earth spins, so each place turns towards the Sun and then away
The Sun switches off at night
Clouds cover the Sun at night
items.why: The Earth spins once in about 24 hours. Each place turns into the sunlight, which is day, then away from it, which is night. Picking 'the Sun goes round' is the old idea that matches what we see, but it is not what happens. Picking 'switches off' or 'clouds' means night is thought of as the Sun stopping. The Sun shines all the time.
items.art: The Earth half lit by the Sun, with a spin arrow.

items.p: The imaginary line that the Earth spins around is called its ____.
items.why: The axis goes through the North Pole and the South Pole. A pencil through an orange is a good model.

items.p: How long does the Earth take to spin round once?
items.why: One spin takes about 24 hours, which is one day and one night. Picking '1 year' mixes up the spin with the Earth's journey round the Sun. That journey takes a year.

items.p: At any moment, about half of the Earth has day and half has night.
items.why: True. The Sun can only light the half of the Earth that faces it.

items.p: In which direction does the Sun seem to rise?
items.why: The Earth turns from west to east, so the Sun seems to come up in the east. Picking 'west' swaps sunrise and sunset.

items.p: The Sun seems to set in the ____.
items.why: The Sun seems to slide across the sky from east to west, so it sets in the west.

items.p: The Sun really moves across the sky every day.
items.why: False. The Sun only seems to move. Our Earth turns, and carries us past the Sun, the way trees seem to rush past a moving train.

items.p: You shine a torch at a ball in a dark room. Which part of the ball is like night?
opts: The side facing away from the torch
items.why: The side facing away from the torch gets no light, like the night side of the Earth. Picking 'the whole ball' forgets that the torch always lights one half.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one mostly happen in the day or at night?
items: bats flying round a street lamp
your long shadow in the evening sunlight
items.why: Owls, bats and fireflies are nocturnal, which means active at night. Sunbirds feed in the day. Clothes dry in sunshine, and shadows from the Sun only happen in the day.

items.p: Why can't we feel the Earth spinning?
opts: Because it is not really spinning
Because the spin is smooth and steady, and everything moves with us
Because it only spins at night
items.why: We feel movement only when it changes, like a bump or a brake. The Earth's spin never bumps or brakes. Picking 'not really spinning' trusts our feelings over the evidence, like Foucault's pendulum. Picking 'only at night' means thinking the spin and the darkness are the same thing.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: our place turns into the sunlight
our place turns away from the sunlight
the Sun is at its highest
the line the Earth spins around
items.why: These are the key words of the unit. Sunrise and sunset are really about our place on the turning Earth.

items.p: Put these in order, starting from early morning: noon, sunrise, night, sunset.
items.why: First our place turns into the light at sunrise. It faces the Sun most at noon. It turns away at sunset. Then it is night until the next sunrise.

items.p: In the morning, the Sun is in the east. Which way does your shadow point?
opts: There is no shadow in the morning
items.why: A shadow always falls on the side away from the light. Picking 'towards the Sun' is a common mix-up. Try it outside tomorrow morning and see.

items.p: Your little cousin says, 'The Sun goes to sleep at night.' What would you tell them? Use the word spin.
items.a: The Sun does not sleep. It shines all the time. Our Earth spins, so at night our side has turned away from the Sun. Children on the other side of the Earth have day then.
items.why: A good answer says the Sun keeps shining, and that the Earth's spin turns us away from it.

items.p: Draw the Sun on one side and the Earth on the other. Shade the night half of the Earth. Draw a small person on the day half.
items.a: The half of the Earth facing the Sun is left bright, with the person on it. The far half is shaded dark.
items.why: The Sun lights the half of the Earth that faces it. The other half is night.
items.art: A blank page with a small circle for the Sun on the left and a bigger circle for the Earth on the right.

items.p: Label the globe: North Pole, South Pole, axis, day side, night side.
items.a: North Pole at the top end of the axis, South Pole at the bottom end. The axis is the line through both. The side facing the Sun is the day side. The side away is the night side.
items.why: These five labels show the whole idea of the unit in one picture.
items.art: A globe with a line through it and a Sun on the left, with five empty label boxes.

items.p: In June, the Sun rises in Dong, Arunachal Pradesh, at about 4 in the morning by the clock. In Bhuj, Kutch, it rises at about 6. Why?
opts: Dong is higher up in the mountains
Dong is further east, so it turns into the sunlight first
The clocks in Dong are wrong
The Sun is closer to Dong
items.why: The Earth turns from west to east, so eastern places turn into the sunlight first. Picking 'higher up' sounds sensible, but height makes only a tiny difference. Picking 'closer to Dong' imagines the Sun as a nearby lamp. It is 150 million kilometres away, the same for both.

items.p: All of India uses one clock time, even though the Sun rises at different times across the country.
items.why: True. India uses Indian Standard Time, set by the Sun near Mirzapur, close to the middle of the country.

items.p: It is 8 at night in Delhi. What is it most likely to be in New York, far to the west, on the other side of the world?
opts: There is no time in New York
items.why: New York is on the other side of the Earth. When India faces away from the Sun, New York is turning into the light. It is about 9:30 or 10:30 in the morning there, depending on the time of year. Picking 'also 8 at night' comes from thinking everyone shares one clock.

items.p: A man in a moving boat sees the trees on the bank move backwards. What did Aryabhata use this example to explain?
opts: Why the stars seem to move west, though it is the Earth that turns
items.why: Aryabhata said the still stars seem to move west because the Earth turns, just as the trees seem to move for the man in the boat. Picking any other answer misses the point of the example: what seems to move is not always what moves.

items.p: In 1851, Léon Foucault showed the Earth spins with a long swinging ____ in Paris.
items.why: His pendulum kept swinging the same way, while the floor and the Earth turned underneath it.

items.p: You set up a pendulum over a stool with a chalk line. You turn the stool slowly while the pendulum swings. What happens?
opts: The pendulum turns with the stool
The pendulum keeps swinging the same way, and the line turns under it
The pendulum swings in a circle
items.why: A pendulum keeps swinging the same way unless something pushes it sideways. Turning the stool does not push the pendulum. So the line turns under the swing. Picking 'turns with the stool' is what most people expect. Try it and see.

items.p: Why does the Pole Star, Dhruva Tara, hardly move in the night sky?
opts: It is stuck to the sky
It sits almost exactly above the North Pole, on the line of the Earth's axis
It is not a real star
items.why: As the Earth spins, the sky seems to turn around the point above the North Pole. Dhruva Tara is almost at that point, so it barely moves. Picking 'the closest star' is a common mix-up. The closest star is the Sun.

items.p: Places near the equator move faster as the Earth spins than places near the poles.
items.why: True. The equator is the fattest part of the Earth, so it has the longest circle to go round in the same 24 hours.

items.p: Long ago, there were about 400 days in a year. What does this tell us?
opts: Each day was shorter, because the Earth spun faster
items.why: The year was about the same length, but it held more days. So each day was shorter, about 22 hours. The Earth's spin has slowed since then. Picking 'the year was longer' is a natural guess, but the year is set by the journey round the Sun, which hardly changed.

items.p: Match each world to its day.
items.why: Every planet spins at its own speed. Jupiter is the fastest. Venus is very slow, and spins backwards.

items.p: After sunset, the sky stays light for a while. Why?
opts: The Sun is still just above the horizon
High air is still catching sunlight and glowing
The clouds keep the light in
items.why: This soft glow is twilight. The Sun is below the horizon for us, but the air high above is still in sunlight. Picking 'the Moon' often comes from linking all night-time light with the Moon.

items.p: Sort these into what is really moving and what only seems to move.
items: stars wheeling round the Pole Star
items.why: When you move, still things seem to move the other way. The Earth and the train really move. The Sun, the trees and the stars only seem to.

items.p: A friend says, 'If the Earth spins so fast, a ball thrown up should land far behind you.' Explain why it does not.
items.a: The ball is already moving with the Earth when I throw it, and so is the air. So it keeps moving along with me and lands back in my hand, like a ball tossed up in a smooth train.
items.why: Galileo used this kind of reasoning in 1632, with a stone dropped from a ship's mast.

items.p: Michel Siffre lived in a cave for two months with no clocks and no daylight. When he came out, he thought far fewer days had passed. What does this tell us about our body clocks?
items.a: We have a body clock that keeps a rough rhythm of sleeping and waking. But without daylight to reset it, it drifts, so he lost count of the days.
items.why: Body clocks run close to 24 hours. Daylight resets them each morning. Without it, they slowly drift.

items.p: Draw the Earth from above the North Pole as a circle. Draw an arrow showing which way it spins. Draw the Sun on the left. Mark where it is sunrise.
items.a: The arrow goes anticlockwise. The Sun is on the left. Sunrise is on the edge where places are just turning from the dark side into the light.
items.why: Seen from above the North Pole, the Earth turns anticlockwise. Sunrise happens on the edge turning towards the Sun.
items.art: An empty circle with a dot in the middle for the North Pole, and a Sun on the left.

items.p: A star rises above a rooftop at 9:00 tonight. When will it rise above the same rooftop tomorrow?
items.why: One spin measured against the stars takes about 23 hours and 56 minutes. So stars come back 4 minutes earlier each night. Picking '9:00 exactly' assumes a spin is exactly 24 hours. Our 24-hour day is measured by the Sun, not the stars.

items.p: In Paris, a Foucault pendulum's swing goes all the way round in about 32 hours. In Delhi it takes about 50 hours. At the North Pole, how long would it take?
items.why: At the North Pole, the floor turns all the way round under the pendulum once a day, so the swing goes round in about 24 hours. Closer to the equator it takes longer. Exactly on the equator, it would not turn at all. Picking 'about 100 hours' follows the wrong direction of the pattern.

items.p: On the equator, a Foucault pendulum's swing would not turn at all.
items.why: True. On the equator, the floor is not turning round under the pendulum the way it is near the poles. It is just carried along. This is one more clue that the turning comes from the Earth.

items.p: On the International Space Station, astronauts see about 16 sunrises every 24 hours. Why?
opts: The Sun moves faster in space
The station goes round the Earth about 16 times a day, in and out of the Earth's shadow
They have very short days because they sleep less
items.why: The station circles the Earth every 90 minutes or so. Each time round, it passes into the Earth's shadow and out again. Picking 'the Sun moves faster in space' still pictures the Sun as the mover.

items.p: The Sun you see touching the horizon at sunset is actually already just below it. Why can you still see it?
opts: The air bends the sunlight a little, lifting the picture of the Sun
items.why: Air bends light a little, like water bends a straw in a glass. Near the horizon, this lifts the picture of the Sun, so we see the Sun for about 2 extra minutes at sunset. Picking 'eyes too slow' is a clever guess about light taking time, but that is a different effect.

items.p: Venus spins very slowly, and backwards compared with the Earth. On Venus, where would the Sun rise?
opts: In the east, like on Earth
items.why: On Earth, we turn west to east, so the Sun seems to come up in the east. Venus turns the other way, so the Sun comes up in the west. Picking 'in the east' means sunrise is thought of as a fixed rule, instead of something made by the spin.

items.p: Fossil corals from 400 million years ago show about 400 days in a year. A year is about 8,760 hours long. Roughly how long was each day? Show your thinking.
items.a: About 22 hours. 8,760 hours shared among 400 days is about 21.9 hours each. With 365 days, it is 24 hours each.
items.why: The same year split into more days means shorter days. This is how scientists worked out that the Earth used to spin faster.

items.p: Why is the night sky dark, when there are billions of stars?
opts: The stars switch off at night
The universe had a beginning, so light from the furthest stars has not reached us, and far light is stretched too dim to see
items.why: This puzzle troubled scientists for centuries. Edgar Allan Poe, a writer, guessed the first part of the answer in 1848. Picking 'clouds' explains why we sometimes see fewer stars, but not why the sky between the stars is black on a clear night. Stars do not switch off at night either. They shine all the time.

items.p: Water in a sink swirls one way in India and the other way in Australia because of the Earth's spin.
items.why: False. A sink is far too small for the spin to matter. The sink's shape and the way the water moved decide the swirl. The spin does turn huge storms, like cyclones.

items.p: Cyclones in the Bay of Bengal spin anticlockwise. Which way do cyclones spin near Australia, south of the equator?
items.why: The Earth's spin turns giant storms one way north of the equator and the other way south of it. Picking 'also anticlockwise' assumes the spin pushes the same way everywhere.

items.p: Aryabhata said the Earth spins in 499 CE. Copernicus said it in 1543. Many books only name Copernicus. Do you think that is fair? Why?
items.a: Any thoughtful answer. For example: it is not fair, because Aryabhata said it more than a thousand years earlier. Or: Copernicus's book changed science in Europe, so he is remembered, but Aryabhata should be named too.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A good answer gives a reason, and knows who said what and when.

items.p: If there were no Moon, scientists think the Earth's spin would slow down…
opts: Much more slowly, because the Moon's tides are the main brake
Not at all, and it would speed up
items.why: The tides made mainly by the Moon rub on the sea floor and brake the spin. With no Moon, the Sun's smaller tides would still brake it a little, but far less. Picking 'much faster' imagines the Moon holding the Earth up.

items.p: Put these in order of who sees the Sun rise first on the same morning: Mumbai, Tokyo, London, Kolkata.
items.why: The Earth turns west to east, so the furthest east sees sunrise first. Tokyo is east of India, then Kolkata, then Mumbai, and London is far to the west.

items.p: Invent a way to tell the time on the Moon, where one day lasts about 29 and a half of our days. Describe it.
items.a: Any good idea. For example: a giant sundial whose shadow moves very slowly, marked in our Earth days. Or a clock that counts Earth hours, because a Moon day is too slow for sleeping by.
items.why: Good answers notice that a Moon day is too long for a person's body clock, and that shadows still move, just very slowly.

items.p: Draw what the night sky looks like in a 2-hour photo pointed at the Pole Star.
items.a: Short curved streaks, like parts of circles, all centred on one bright point near the middle, which is the Pole Star.
items.why: As the Earth turns, all the stars seem to circle the point above the North Pole. In 2 hours, each star moves one-twelfth of the way round.
items.art: A dark empty square with one small star near the middle.

experiments.title: Torch and Ball: where does the night come from?
experiments.context: This is the torch and ball experiment. You shine a torch at a ball in a dark room, and turn the ball slowly. You find out how day and night happen, and which places see the Sun first.
experiments.question: Can a torch that stays still, and a ball that turns, make day and night? And which place sees the sunrise first?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Put three stickers on the ball for Dong, your home and Bhuj. Which sticker will come into the light first when you turn the ball, Dong in the east or Bhuj in the west? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, keep the torch still in one place the whole time. Only the ball moves. Turn it the same slow way each time, from west to east. Try it 3 times, because one try can be a mistake.
results_table: How much of the ball was lit (about half? more? less?)

materials.item: an orange or a mausambi (or a small globe, if you have one)
a pencil or a knitting needle to push through it, for the axis (a grown-up does the pushing)
a torch (a phone torch works)
3 small stickers or bindis, and a pen
a dark room

experiments.safety: A grown-up pushes the pencil or needle through the fruit. Do not shine the torch into anyone's eyes.

schedule.what: Make the Earth ball. Shine the torch. Turn the ball and watch day and night. Find who sees the Sun first. Finish with claim, evidence and reasoning.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for 3 tries. Then draw the ball and the torch, and shade the night half.

setup.art: An orange with a pencil pushed through it from top to bottom, and three small bindis stuck on its side in a row.
setup.caption: 1. Push a pencil through the ball. Stick on three dots: Dong, home and Bhuj.

setup.art: A dark room with a torch on a pile of books shining at the orange held up by its pencil, half of the orange bright.
setup.caption: 2. Put the torch on a pile of books. Shine it at the ball. Keep the torch still, on your right side.

setup.art: A child's hands turning the pencil so the orange spins, with a curved arrow showing the direction, and one dot just coming into the light.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the ball slowly from west to east. Watch which dot comes into the light first.

flow.do: Ask your child where the Sun goes at night. Write down their answer, without correcting it.
flow.say: Where do you think the Sun goes at night? Tell me your idea. I'll write it down, and we'll test it.
flow.kid: Where does the Sun go at night? Say your idea. Write it down. We will test it.
flow.parent: All answers are welcome. Many children say the Sun goes behind the hills, into the sea, or to sleep. Keep their answer. They will check it themselves at the end.
flow.context: This is the first step of the torch and ball experiment. First, your child shares their own idea of where the Sun goes at night.

flow.do: 1. Push the pencil through the fruit, from top to bottom. 2. Tell your child the top is the North Pole. 3. Stick three dots in a row a little above the middle, about two finger-widths apart. As you look at it, put Dong on the right, home in the middle and Bhuj on the left.
flow.say: This ball is the Earth. The pencil is its axis, the line it spins around. The top is the North Pole. These dots are three places in India.
flow.kid: This ball is the Earth. The pencil is its axis. The top is the North Pole. Stick on three dots for three places.
flow.parent: Seen from the front, with the North Pole on top, east is to the right on the ball. So Dong goes to the right of Bhuj, with your home in between. India is north of the equator, so the dots go a little above the middle. The real places are closer together than this, but spacing them out makes the order easy to see.

flow.do: 1. Make the room dark. 2. Put the torch on a pile of books, shining at the ball. 3. Hold the ball still by its pencil, about an arm's length from the torch. 4. Sit beside the ball so the torch shines on it from your right side.
flow.say: The torch is the Sun. Look at the ball. How much of it is lit up?
flow.kid: Turn off the lights. Shine the torch at the ball. How much of the ball is bright?

ask.q: How much of the ball is lit?
good: The side facing the torch is bright, and the back is dark.

check.q: The torch shines at the ball. How much of the ball is lit?
options: About half, the side facing the torch
check.why: Light travels in straight lines, so it can only reach the side facing the torch. The back is in the ball's own shadow. The real Earth is the same. Half has day, and half has night. Picking 'a small spot' usually comes from looking only at the brightest part. Look again at the edges.

flow.do: 1. Turn the ball slowly by its pencil, so the front moves from left to right. That is west to east. 2. Stop each time a dot crosses into the light. 3. Write it in the table. 4. Do it 3 times.
flow.say: Now the Earth spins. Turn it slowly, west to east. Which dot comes into the sunlight first?
flow.kid: Turn the ball slowly by the pencil. Which dot comes into the light first? Write it down. Do it 3 times.
flow.parent: Dong should come into the light first, then home, then Bhuj. If it goes the other way, the ball is turning the wrong way. Check that the torch is on your right, and turn the ball so the side facing you moves from left to right.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Turn the ball until Dong is just going into the dark, while Bhuj is still in the light.
flow.say: Look. Here it is already night in Dong, but still evening in Bhuj. Did the torch move at all?
flow.kid: Turn until Dong is in the dark. Is Bhuj still in the light? Did the torch move?

check.q: In the experiment, what made the dots go from day into night?
check.why: The torch stayed still on its books the whole time. Only the ball turned. So day and night came from the turning. Picking 'the torch moving' is the everyday feeling that the Sun travels. Picking 'dimmer' imagines night as the Sun fading. It never fades.

flow.think: Right now, is somebody on the real Earth just going into the night?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Then read their first answer from step 1 together.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think makes night? What did you see that shows it? Why does it happen? Now let's read your first idea. Would you change it?
flow.kid: Now say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why. Then read your first idea. Would you change it?
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: night comes because the Earth turns away from the Sun. What I saw: the torch never moved, but the dots went into the dark when I turned the ball. Why: light only reaches the side facing the Sun.

experiments.title: The Shadow Stick: does the Sun really move across the sky?
experiments.context: This is the shadow stick experiment. You stand a stick in the sun and mark the tip of its shadow every hour. The shadow moves and changes length, and you find out why.
experiments.question: How does a stick's shadow change during one day? What does it tell us about the Sun and the Earth?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the shadow be longest in the morning, at noon or in the afternoon? Which way will it move? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, the stick must not move all day. Mark the shadow from the same stick at the same spot each time. Mark it every hour, on the hour, by the clock.

materials.item: a straight stick about 30 cm long, such as a bamboo stick (a pencil works too, but its shadows will be shorter)
a flowerpot of soil, or a lump of atta dough or clay, to hold it upright
a big sheet of paper, such as an opened newspaper, or a spot of floor you can draw on with chalk
a ruler and a clock

experiments.safety: Never look straight at the Sun, not even for a moment. Look only at the shadow. Wear a cap in the midday sun, and drink water.

schedule.what: Set the stick up in the morning. Spend about 2 minutes every hour marking the shadow tip, from about 9 until 4. At the end, measure and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a line from the stick to each mark. Then draw a line chart of shadow length against clock time.

setup.art: A stick standing straight up in a pot of soil on a sunny terrace, on a big sheet of paper.
setup.caption: 1. Stand a stick straight up in a sunny spot that stays sunny all day.

setup.art: A child's hand making a chalk cross at the tip of the stick's long morning shadow, with the time 9:00 written beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Every hour, mark the tip of the shadow. Write the time next to it.

setup.art: The sheet at the end of the day, with a curved fan of crosses around the stick, long ones at each end and short ones in the middle.
setup.caption: 3. At the end, measure each shadow. Which was shortest?

flow.do: 1. In the morning, find the spot that gets the most sun: a balcony, a terrace or a sunny window sill. 2. Stand the stick straight up in the pot. 3. Put the paper under it, and weigh the corners down with books or steel tumblers.
flow.say: This stick will be our clock. Do you think its shadow will stay the same all day?
flow.kid: Stand the stick straight up in a sunny spot. Put the paper under it. Will its shadow stay the same all day?
flow.parent: Never let anyone look at the Sun itself. Shadows tell us everything we need. If no spot in your home gets sun all day, mark only the hours it does. Even three marks an hour apart show the shadow moving.
flow.context: This is the first step of the shadow stick experiment. You set up a stick in a sunny spot to watch its shadow all day.

flow.do: 1. Every hour, mark the tip of the shadow with a cross. 2. Write the clock time next to it. 3. Measure the shadow from the stick to the cross, and write it in the table.
flow.say: It's on the hour. Let's mark the tip of the shadow, and measure it.
flow.kid: Every hour, mark the tip of the shadow. Write the time. Measure it with the ruler. Write it in the table.
flow.parent: Set an alarm on a phone for each hour. About 2 minutes each time is enough. If clouds come, skip that hour and carry on.
flow.wait: Come back every hour until about 4 in the afternoon.

flow.do: Look at all the marks together.
flow.say: Look at all the crosses. When was the shadow longest? When was it shortest? Which way did it move?
flow.kid: Look at all your crosses. When was the shadow longest? When was it shortest? Which way did it swing?

ask.q: Why was the shadow short around noon?
good: Because the Sun was high in the sky.
Because the light came from above, so the stick blocked only a little.

check.q: In the shadow stick experiment, when was the shadow shortest?
check.why: Around noon the Sun is highest, so the light comes from nearly above, and the stick blocks only a little of it. Picking 'early morning' usually means thinking the morning sun is the strongest. In fact a low Sun makes the longest shadows.

chart.title: Made-up example: shadow length through one day
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different. Where you live, and the time of year, change them.

flow.do: Ask: is the Sun moving, or are we? Take the ball and torch from the torch and ball experiment. Push a tiny matchstick into the ball as a stick.
flow.say: The shadow moved because the Sun seemed to move across the sky. But remember the ball and the torch. Let's put a tiny stick on our ball and turn it.
flow.kid: Push a tiny stick into your Earth ball. Shine the torch. Turn the ball. Watch the tiny shadow move!
flow.think: If the torch stays still and the ball turns, does the little shadow still move?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think made the shadow move? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Now say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the shadow moves because the Earth turns, so the Sun seems to cross the sky. What I saw: the shadow was 40 cm at 9, only 8 cm at 1, then long again by 4. It swung from one side to the other. Why: when the Sun is low, the stick blocks a long strip of light.

example_chart.note: Made-up numbers. In India, the shortest shadow often comes after 12 by the clock, especially in the west of the country.

experiments.title: Foucault's Pendulum on a Stool
experiments.context: This is a small home version of Foucault's pendulum. You hang a weight on a string over a stool and turn the stool while the weight swings. It shows how scientists proved the Earth spins.
experiments.question: If the floor turns under a swinging pendulum, does the swing turn with it?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. When we turn the stool, will the pendulum's swing turn with it, or stay the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, start the swing along the chalk line every time. Turn the stool very slowly and smoothly, so you do not shake the string. Try it 3 times.
results_table: Did the swing stay the same way, or turn with the stool?
Where the swing was at the end, compared with the chalk line

materials.item: a string about 1 metre long
something heavy and small to tie on the end, like a bunch of keys or a big nut
a round stool you can slide round on the floor, or a big steel plate (a thali) on a smooth floor
a chalk or a strip of paper to mark a line on the stool
a broom handle laid across the backs of two chairs, or a table edge, to hang the string from

experiments.safety: Tie the weight on tightly. Keep faces away from the swinging weight.

schedule.what: Hang the pendulum over the stool. Start it swinging along a line. Turn the stool slowly and watch. Then learn about Foucault's real pendulum.

experiments.record: Draw the stool from above, with the chalk line, at the start and at the end. Draw an arrow for the swing each time.

setup.art: A heavy nut tied to a string hanging from a stick laid across two chairs, just above the seat of a round stool with a chalk line across it.
setup.caption: 1. Hang the weight so it just clears the stool. Wind up extra string on the handle. Draw a line across the stool.

setup.art: The weight swinging to and fro exactly along the chalk line, dotted arc showing its swing.
setup.caption: 2. Start it swinging along the line.

setup.art: Hands slowly turning the stool a quarter turn while the weight keeps swinging the same way, the chalk line now crossways to the swing.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the stool slowly a quarter turn. Watch the swing and the line.

flow.do: 1. Tie the weight to the string. 2. Tie the other end to a broom handle laid across the backs of two chairs. Wind the extra string round the handle until the weight hangs just above the stool or plate, without touching it. 3. Draw a chalk line across the middle of the stool or plate.
flow.say: This is a pendulum, a weight on a string. Let's see what it does when the floor under it turns.
flow.kid: Tie the weight to the string. Hang it just above the stool. Draw a line across the stool.
flow.context: This is the first step of the pendulum experiment. You hang a weight on a string over a stool that can turn.

flow.do: 1. Pull the weight to one end of the chalk line, and let it go gently, without pushing it sideways. 2. When it swings neatly along the line, turn the stool very slowly a quarter turn. 3. Do it 3 times.
flow.say: Now I'll turn the stool very slowly. Watch the swing. Does it turn with the stool?
flow.kid: Let the weight swing along the line. Now turn the stool very slowly. Watch the swing closely.

check.q: When the stool turned, what did the pendulum's swing do?
options: It kept swinging the same way, and the line turned under it
check.why: A swinging pendulum keeps swinging the same way unless something pushes it sideways. Turning the stool does not push the weight. So the line turns away under the swing. Picking 'turned with the stool' is what most people expect. That is why this test is so surprising.

flow.do: Tell your child about Foucault's real pendulum in Paris.
flow.say: In 1851, Léon Foucault hung a heavy ball on a 67-metre wire in a great hall in Paris. Nobody turned the floor. But over the hours, the swing seemed to turn round the room. What was turning?
flow.kid: In 1851, Foucault hung a giant pendulum in Paris. Nobody turned the floor. But the swing seemed to turn. What was really turning?

ask.q: In Paris, what was really turning?
good: The floor, because the whole Earth was turning.
The Earth turned under the pendulum, like our stool.

flow.parent: In Paris the swing goes all the way round in about 32 hours. In Delhi, it takes about 50 hours. India's new Parliament building has one, opened in 2023.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think the pendulum does when the floor turns? What did you see? Why?
flow.kid: Now say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a pendulum keeps swinging the same way, so a turning floor shows up. What I saw: the line turned a quarter turn, but the swing stayed pointing at the window. Why: nothing pushed the weight sideways. So Foucault's pendulum shows the Earth turning.

activities.title: Be the Earth
activities.context: This is a short activity where your child becomes the spinning Earth. A grown-up is the Sun. When the child faces the grown-up, it is day. When they turn away, it is night.

materials.item: a lamp or a grown-up to be the Sun
a bit of open space

activities.safety: Turn slowly so nobody gets dizzy. Clear away anything you could bump into.

schedule.what: Act out the Earth's spin, then its journey round the Sun.

activities.record: Draw yourself as the Earth, with your face in the light and your back in the dark.

setup.art: A parent standing still with arms open like a glowing Sun, and a child facing them, smiling.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up stands still. They are the Sun.

setup.art: The child turning slowly on the spot, a curved arrow around them, their back now to the parent.
setup.caption: 2. The child turns slowly on the spot. Face the Sun: day. Back to it: night.

setup.art: The child slowly walking in a big circle around the parent while still turning on the spot.
setup.caption: 3. Bonus: turn and walk round the Sun at the same time.

flow.do: 1. Stand still in the middle of the room. You are the Sun. 2. Your child stands facing you, a few steps away.
flow.say: I am the Sun. I am going to stand very still. You are the Earth. Your nose is our home town.
flow.kid: A grown-up is the Sun and stands still. You are the Earth. Your nose is your town.
flow.context: This is the first step of Be the Earth. Your child acts as the spinning Earth to feel how day and night happen.

flow.do: Ask your child to turn very slowly on the spot, to their left, which is anticlockwise. Call out as they turn.
flow.say: Turn slowly. Can your nose see the Sun? Then it's day at home. Now your nose is turning away. Sunset! Now it's night. Keep turning. Here comes the Sun again. Sunrise!
flow.kid: Turn slowly to your left. Can your nose see the Sun? It is day! Turning away? Sunset. Back to the Sun? Sunrise!

check.q: When was it night for your nose?
options: When my back was to the Sun
check.why: The Sun stood still the whole time. It was night when your nose had turned away from it. That is how the real Earth works. Picking 'when the Sun walked away' is the old idea that the Sun goes round us.

flow.do: Now try both movements at once: your child keeps turning, and also walks slowly in a big circle round you. Count the turns.
flow.say: The real Earth does two things. It spins, and it also travels round the Sun. It spins about 365 times on one trip round. Let's try just a few!
flow.kid: Now turn and walk around the Sun at the same time. Count your spins. The real Earth spins 365 times on one trip!
flow.parent: Go slowly. Spinning makes day and night. Travelling round the Sun takes a year. This helps your child feel the difference.
flow.think: Which takes longer, one spin or one trip round the Sun?

activities.title: The Train Window Trick
activities.context: This activity shows how something can seem to move when it is really you who moves. It is the same trick that makes the Sun seem to cross the sky.

materials.item: a swivel chair, or a safe spot to turn slowly on your feet
a car, bus or train ride, if you have one coming up

activities.safety: Spin slowly and stop if you feel dizzy. Never lean out of a moving vehicle.

schedule.what: Spin slowly on a chair and watch the room. Next time you ride in a vehicle, watch the trees.

activities.record: Draw what you saw from the chair or the window, with arrows for which way things seemed to move.

setup.art: A child sitting on a swivel chair, a grown-up gently turning it, the room drawn with blurry arrows going the other way.
setup.caption: 1. Sit on a swivel chair. A grown-up turns it slowly.

setup.art: A child at a bus window, trees and poles outside with arrows pointing backwards.
setup.caption: 2. On a ride, look out of the side window at the trees.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits on a swivel chair, looking straight ahead. 2. Turn the chair very slowly to the left.
flow.say: Keep your eyes looking straight ahead. Which way does the room seem to move?
flow.kid: Sit still and look straight ahead. The chair turns slowly. Which way does the room seem to slide?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Train Window Trick. Your child turns slowly on a chair and watches the room seem to move.

flow.do: Explain Aryabhata's boat example.
flow.say: About 1,500 years ago, Aryabhata wrote this. A man in a boat sees the trees on the bank moving backwards. In the same way, we see the stars moving west. But it is the Earth that turns.
flow.kid: Long ago, Aryabhata said this. From a boat, trees seem to move backwards. The stars seem to move west, the same way. Really, the Earth turns.

check.q: You turn left on a chair. The room seems to slide right. What is really moving?
check.why: The room stayed still. You turned, so the room seemed to slide the other way. The Sun and stars work the same way: the Earth turns east, so they seem to move west. Picking 'the room' trusts the feeling over the facts.

flow.do: On your next ride in a bus, car or train, remind your child to look out of the side window.
flow.say: Look out of the window. Are the trees running? Or are we?
flow.kid: On your next ride, look out of the window. Are the trees running away? Or are you moving?
flow.think: If you could not see out, and the ride was perfectly smooth, would you know you were moving?

activities.title: Sunrise and Sunset Diary
activities.context: This is a week-long diary of when the Sun rises and sets where you live. You write down the times, find out how long each day of light is, and compare your town with others.

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
sunrise and sunset times from a newspaper, a weather app or timeanddate.com
a window or terrace facing east or west, if you have one

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun. Look at the sky near it, or at the light on buildings.

schedule.what: Set up the diary. Write today's sunrise and sunset times.
Write today's times. Watch one sunset from a window, if you can.
Write today's times. Look up the times for one city far to the east and one far to the west.
Write today's times. Work out how many hours of daylight you had, and compare.

activities.record: A table with the date, sunrise time, sunset time and hours of daylight, for 7 days.

setup.art: A notebook open to a table with columns drawn for date, sunrise and sunset, a pencil beside it, and a phone showing a weather app.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a table. Find today's sunrise and sunset times.

setup.art: A child at a window watching the sky turn orange behind buildings, holding the notebook.
setup.caption: 2. Watch a sunset if you can. Write the times every day.

flow.do: Help your child draw a table with 4 columns: date, sunrise, sunset, hours of light. Find today's times.
flow.say: Every day this week, we'll write down when the Sun rises and sets here. Let's see if the times change.
flow.kid: Draw a table. Date, sunrise, sunset, hours of light. Write today's times. Do it every day this week.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sunrise and Sunset Diary. You start a table of the Sun's times for one week.

flow.do: Each day, add the times. On day 3, watch a sunset together.
flow.say: Let's write today's times. Did sunrise come a little earlier or later than yesterday?
flow.kid: Write today's times. Is sunrise earlier or later than yesterday?
flow.wait: Write the times every day for a week.
flow.parent: The times change by about a minute a day, or less. Which way they change depends on the time of year. That is part of the seasons unit.

flow.do: On day 7, work out the hours of daylight. Then look up today's sunrise in a city far east and far west of you.
flow.say: Say sunrise was at 6 in the morning and sunset at 6 in the evening. How many hours of light is that? Now, when did the Sun rise in Guwahati and in Ahmedabad today?
flow.kid: Count the hours from sunrise to sunset. Now find sunrise in a city far east, and far west. Which was first?

check.q: Guwahati is far east of Ahmedabad. Whose sunrise comes first?
check.why: The Earth turns west to east, so Guwahati turns into the sunlight first, more than an hour before Ahmedabad. Picking 'the same time' comes from India having one clock time.

activities.title: What Is Happening Around the World Right Now?
activities.context: In this activity, you find out what time it is in other places right now, and what people there are doing. Then you mark it on your Earth ball to see why.

materials.item: a world clock on a phone, or a friend or relative abroad to call
the Earth ball and the torch from the torch and ball experiment
a world map or globe

activities.safety: Call people only with a grown-up, and only at a sensible time for them.

schedule.what: Check the time in 4 places. Guess what people are doing there. Find each place on the ball.

activities.record: Write 4 places, their time now, and whether it is day or night there.

setup.art: A phone showing a world clock with four cities and their times, next to a small globe.
setup.caption: 1. Look up the time now in 4 places around the world.

setup.art: The orange Earth ball under torchlight with small paper flags on toothpicks, some in the light and some in the dark.
setup.caption: 2. Put a small flag on the ball for each place. Which are in the light?

flow.do: Look up the time now in London, New York, Tokyo and Sydney.
flow.say: It's our time now. What time do you think it is in New York? Let's check.
flow.kid: Guess the time in New York right now. Now check. Were you close?
flow.context: This is the first step of What Is Happening Around the World Right Now? You look up the time in other countries.

flow.do: For each place, guess what people are doing: sleeping, eating breakfast, at school or having dinner.
flow.say: If it is 3 in the morning in New York, what are the children there doing?
flow.kid: For each place, guess what children there are doing right now. Sleeping? At school?

ask.q: Why is it a different time there?
good: Because their side of the Earth is facing a different way.
Because the Earth spins, so they are in the dark while we are in the light.

flow.do: Put small paper flags on the ball for each place. Shine the torch so India is in the light. Check which flags are in the dark.
flow.say: Let's put India in the torchlight. Where are New York and London now?
flow.kid: Shine the torch on India. Is New York in the light, or the dark?
flow.think: If you call a friend in New York at bedtime, what will they be doing?

activities.title: The Star Clock: stars turning round Dhruva Tara
activities.context: This is a night-time activity. You draw the stars near the Pole Star twice, two hours apart, and see that they have turned around it. It is evidence that the Earth spins.

materials.item: a clear night with a view of the northern sky
paper, a pencil and a coloured pencil
a phone with a night or long-exposure camera mode, if you have one

activities.safety: Go out at night only with a grown-up. Stay in a safe, familiar place.

schedule.what: After dark, draw the Saptarishi and the Pole Star with a rooftop. Draw them again 2 hours later.

activities.record: One drawing with two sets of stars in two colours, and the rooftop or tree that stayed still.

setup.art: A child and parent on a terrace at night, the parent pointing to the seven stars of the Saptarishi low in the north, a rooftop below.
setup.caption: 1. Find the Saptarishi in the northern sky. Follow the two pointer stars to Dhruva Tara.

setup.art: A drawing on paper of the Saptarishi and the Pole Star above a rooftop, labelled with the time 8:00.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the stars and a rooftop. Write the time.

setup.art: The same drawing with a second set of Saptarishi stars in a different colour, swung round the Pole Star, labelled 10:00.
setup.caption: 3. Two hours later, from the same spot, draw them again in a new colour.

flow.do: 1. After dark, go out to a spot with a view north. 2. Find the Saptarishi, seven bright stars shaped like a big ladle. 3. Follow the two stars at the end of the ladle's cup to the Pole Star. 4. Draw them, with a rooftop or tree below. Write the time.
flow.say: Those seven stars are the Saptarishi. The two at the end point to Dhruva Tara, the Pole Star. Let's draw them, and the rooftop.
flow.kid: Find the seven stars of the Saptarishi. The two end stars point to Dhruva Tara. Draw them. Draw a rooftop too.
flow.parent: The Saptarishi is easiest to see in the evening from about February to June. In other months, look for Cassiopeia, a W shape, on the other side of the Pole Star. In very southern India, the Pole Star is low, near the horizon.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Star Clock. You draw the stars around the Pole Star so you can see them turn.

flow.do: Two hours later, stand in exactly the same spot. Draw the stars again on the same paper, in a new colour.
flow.say: Same spot, same rooftop. Have the stars moved?
flow.kid: Two hours later, stand in the same spot. Draw the stars again in a new colour. Have they moved?

flow.do: Compare the two drawings. Look at what moved and what stayed still.
flow.say: The rooftop stayed still. The Saptarishi swung round the Pole Star. But the Pole Star stayed put. Why?
flow.kid: The rooftop did not move. The Saptarishi swung round. Did the Pole Star move?

check.q: Why did the Saptarishi stars swing round the Pole Star?
options: The stars are flying round it
The Earth is turning, and the Pole Star is above the North Pole
check.why: The Earth turns, so the whole sky seems to turn around the point above the North Pole. Dhruva Tara sits almost at that point. Picking 'the stars are flying' is the same mix-up as thinking the Sun goes round us.

flow.think: In 24 hours, how far round would the Saptarishi go?

activities.title: See the Earth's Own Shadow
activities.context: This is a sunset activity. Just after sunset, you look east, away from the Sun, and see a dark band low in the sky. It is the shadow of the whole Earth.

materials.item: a clear evening and a view of the eastern sky, from a terrace, a window facing east, a beach or a field
a pencil and blue and pink crayons

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun. Turn your back to it, and look east. Go out only with a grown-up.

schedule.what: Go out at sunset. Turn your back to the Sun. Watch the eastern sky for about 8 minutes.

activities.record: A drawing of the eastern sky after sunset, with the dark blue band and the pink band above it.

setup.art: A child on a terrace at sunset with their back to the orange setting Sun, facing the eastern sky.
setup.caption: 1. At sunset, turn your back to the Sun. Face east.

setup.art: The eastern sky after sunset: a dark blue-grey band along the horizon, a pink glowing band above it, a child pointing.
setup.caption: 2. Look for a dark blue band low down, with a pink band above it.

flow.do: Just as the Sun sets, stand with your backs to it. Face east.
flow.say: The Sun is setting behind us. Let's look the other way, east, and watch the sky low down.
flow.kid: The Sun is setting behind you. Turn your back to it. Look east, low in the sky.
flow.context: This is the first step of See the Earth's Own Shadow. You face away from the setting Sun to look for the Earth's shadow.

flow.do: Watch for about 8 minutes. Look for a dark blue band along the horizon, rising slowly, with a pink band above it.
flow.say: See that dark blue band? That's the shadow of the whole Earth, falling on the air. We are inside it now, turning into the night.
flow.kid: See the dark blue band low down? That is the Earth's own shadow. Watch it rise slowly.

ask.q: Why does the shadow band rise?
good: Because the Earth is turning us further into its own shadow.
Because our side is turning away from the Sun.

flow.parent: The pink band above the shadow is sometimes called the Belt of Venus. It is sunlight still lighting the high air. On hazy city evenings, it can be faint. A beach or open field helps.

flow.do: Draw what you saw.
flow.say: Let's draw it. Where is the Sun? Where is the shadow?
flow.kid: Draw the sky. Colour the shadow band blue and the band above it pink.

check.q: What is the dark band low in the eastern sky just after sunset?
options: The shadow of the Earth on the air
check.why: The Earth blocks the sunlight and casts a shadow, just like a ball under a torch. After sunset, we can see that shadow on the air in the east. Picking 'a cloud' or 'smoke' is a fair guess, but the band is there on clear evenings everywhere, and it always faces away from the Sun.

projects.title: Build a Sundial and Find Your Own Noon
projects.context: This is a three-day project. You build a sundial, a clock that uses the Sun's shadow. Then you find your town's true noon, and see why it is not always 12 by the clock.

materials.item: a stiff paper plate or a round piece of cardboard
a pencil or straw, for the stick that makes the shadow
a lump of clay or dough to hold it upright
a marker, a clock and a compass app or a known east-west direction

projects.safety: Never look straight at the Sun. Wear a cap in the midday sun.

schedule.what: Build the sundial. Put it in a sunny spot. Mark the shadow every hour.
Check the sundial against the clock at three times in the day.
Find the time of the shortest shadow. That is your true noon. Compare it with 12 by the clock, and with other towns.

projects.record: The sundial plate with hour marks, and a note of the clock time when the shadow was shortest.

setup.art: A paper plate with a pencil pushed straight up through its centre, held in a lump of clay, on a sunny windowsill.
setup.caption: 1. Push a pencil up through the centre of a paper plate.

setup.art: The plate with marker lines drawn along the shadow at each hour, numbered 9, 10, 11, 12, 1, 2, 3.
setup.caption: 2. Every hour, draw along the shadow and write the clock time.

setup.art: A child checking a wristwatch while looking at the shortest shadow on the plate.
setup.caption: 3. Find when the shadow is shortest. That is your true noon.

flow.do: 1. Push the pencil straight up through the middle of the plate. 2. Stand it in a lump of clay. 3. Put it in a spot that will be sunny all day. 4. Mark where the plate sits, so you can put it back in the same place tomorrow.
flow.say: People told the time with shadows for thousands of years before clocks. Let's make our own Sun clock.
flow.kid: Push the pencil through the plate's middle. Stand it up in clay. Put it in a sunny spot.
flow.context: This is the first step of the sundial project. You build a clock that tells the time with a shadow.

flow.do: Every hour on the hour, draw a line along the shadow and write the clock time at its end.
flow.say: It's 10 o'clock. Let's draw along the shadow and write 10.
flow.kid: Every hour, draw a line along the shadow. Write the time at the end.
flow.wait: Mark the shadow every hour for the rest of the day.

flow.do: The next day, put the sundial back in the same place. Read the time from the shadow, then check the clock.
flow.say: What time does our sundial say? And the clock? Are they close?
flow.kid: Put the sundial back in its spot. What time does the shadow say? Check the clock.
flow.wait: Do this on the second day.

flow.do: On day 3, from 11:30 to 1:30, check the shadow every 15 minutes. Find when it is shortest.
flow.say: The shortest shadow is the Sun's true noon here. Is it at 12 by the clock?
flow.kid: Check the shadow every 15 minutes around midday. When is it shortest? That is your true noon.
flow.parent: In most of India, true noon is not at 12 by the clock. In Kolkata it comes between about 11:20 and 11:50, depending on the time of year. In Mumbai it comes between about 12:20 and 12:55. India's clock time is set by the Sun near Mirzapur, in Uttar Pradesh. Places west of it have later noons.

check.q: Your sundial's shortest shadow came at 12:40 by the clock. Why might that be?
options: Your town is west of the line India's clock time is set by
check.why: India's clock time is set by the Sun near Mirzapur. Places to the west turn under the Sun later, so their true noon comes after 12. Picking 'the Sun was late' still pictures the Sun as the thing that moves.

flow.do: Look up true noon for a town far east and far west of you. Talk about it.
flow.say: When is true noon in Guwahati? And in Ahmedabad? Why are they different?
flow.kid: Find true noon in a far-east town and a far-west town. Why are they different?
flow.think: If every town set its clocks by its own noon, what would happen to train timetables?

challenges.title: Morning at the Midnight Sun
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In summer, at India's Arctic research station, the Sun never sets. You design a way for the scientists there to know when to sleep and when to wake.
challenges.problem: At Himadri, India's research station in Svalbard in the Arctic, the Sun does not set at all from about the middle of April to late August. The scientists still need to sleep about 8 hours and work in the day. Design something that tells them when it is 'night' and helps them sleep.
constraints: It cannot use the Sun to tell the time, because the Sun is up all day and all night.
It must help people's body clocks, not just tell the time.
Draw it, and make a small model from things at home.
materials: a shoebox, a torch and coloured cellophane or cloth
general: Thick dark curtains, called blackout curtains, keep the bedroom dark.
Eye masks block light from your eyes.
Everyone agrees to follow one clock, and sticks to the same bedtime every day.
Keep the bedroom cool and quiet.
creative: A lamp that slowly turns orange and dim in the evening, like a sunset, and bright white in the morning.
A 'sunset song' that plays at bedtime, so the body learns the signal.
Grow a touch-me-not plant inside. Its leaves fold at its own 'night', like a living clock.
Astronauts on the space station see 16 sunsets a day. They use special lights that change colour to help their body clocks.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Draw it, make a model in a shoebox, and test it on your family for one evening. Did it help anyone feel sleepy?

setup.art: A small red research hut in a snowy Arctic place, the Sun low in the sky at midnight, a clock on the wall showing 12.
setup.caption: 1. Picture it: at midnight, the Sun is still in the sky.

setup.art: A shoebox bedroom model with a dark cloth curtain and a torch covered in orange cellophane.
setup.caption: 2. Design and build a model to make night inside.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the art of the Sun at midnight.
flow.say: Imagine the Sun is still up at midnight. How would you know it was time for bed?
flow.kid: Imagine the Sun never sets. How would you know it is bedtime?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Morning at the Midnight Sun challenge. You find out about places where the Sun does not set for weeks.

flow.do: List three ideas together before building anything.
flow.say: Engineers think before they build. Let's list three ideas.
flow.kid: Think like an engineer. Draw three ideas before you build.

flow.do: Build a shoebox model of the best idea, with a dark curtain or a coloured light.
flow.say: Let's build a little bedroom in a shoebox, and test if it can make a night inside.
flow.kid: Build your best idea in a shoebox. Can you make it dark inside, even in daylight?
flow.parent: A torch covered with orange cellophane makes a gentle sunset light. Peek through a small hole to check how dark the box gets.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative solutions together.
flow.say: Here's what people really do, and some creative ideas. Can you invent something better?
flow.kid: Look at what people really do. Now invent your own. Can you beat them?
flow.think: Do you think animals in the Arctic sleep less in summer? How could we find out?

challenges.title: Day and Night You Can Feel
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You make a model of day and night for a friend who cannot see. They should be able to feel how the spinning Earth makes day and night.
challenges.problem: Your friend is blind. Design a model they can touch and feel, to show that day and night happen because the Earth spins.
constraints: It must work without eyes, using touch, warmth or sound.
It must show that the Sun stays still and the Earth turns.
Use things you have at home.
materials: a ball and a pencil for an axis
sunshine from a window, or a lamp with an old-style bulb that gets warm
bumpy stickers, buttons, or a dab of glue to mark places
general: Use warmth instead of light. The side of a ball facing a warm lamp or the sun gets warm. The far side stays cool.
Stick a bump, like a button, on the ball for your town, so your friend can feel where 'home' is.
Let your friend turn the ball themselves by its axis.
creative: Tie a small bell near 'home' that rings when it turns into the warm side, like a rooster at sunrise.
Use a cool, damp cloth for the night side and a warm cloth for the day side.
Let your friend stand and turn in the sunshine, feeling the warmth on their face and then the back of their head.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Make it, then test it with your eyes closed. Can you feel when 'home' has day?

setup.art: A ball on a pencil axis with a button stuck on it, held near a warm lamp, a child with eyes closed touching the warm side.
setup.caption: 1. Mark 'home' with a bump. Hold the ball near a warm lamp.

setup.art: A child with eyes closed turning the ball by its pencil, feeling the button move from the warm side to the cool side.
setup.caption: 2. Turn the ball with your eyes shut. Feel home go from warm to cool.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Close your eyes for a minute and talk about how you know it is day without seeing.
flow.say: Close your eyes. How could you tell it is day, without seeing anything?
flow.kid: Close your eyes. How can you tell it is day, without looking?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Day and Night You Can Feel challenge. You think about how someone who cannot see could know about day and night.

flow.do: 1. Mark 'home' on the ball with a button. 2. Hold it near a warm lamp or in sunshine. 3. With eyes closed, turn the ball and feel the button warm up and cool down.
flow.say: Shut your eyes. Turn the ball slowly. Feel for the button. Is it warm or cool?
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Turn the ball slowly. Find the button. Is it warm? Then it is day there.
flow.parent: A sunny window works best. An old-style bulb that gets warm also works. Do not let anyone touch a hot bulb. LED bulbs give off very little warmth, so sunshine may work better.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative ideas. Then improve your model.
flow.say: Here are some ideas. Can you make yours even better, so your friend could really understand it?
flow.kid: Look at the ideas. Now make your model even better. Test it with your eyes shut.
flow.think: Sunlight brings warmth as well as light. What else does it bring to the Earth?

quiz.p: Why do we have day and night?
opts: The Sun goes round the Earth
The Earth spins, so each place faces the Sun and then faces away
The Moon blocks the Sun at night
The Sun goes out at night
quiz.why: The Earth spins once in about 24 hours. Each place turns into the sunlight, then out of it. Picking 'the Sun goes round' is the oldest mix-up of all. It matches what we see, but not what happens. Picking 'the Moon blocks it' mixes night up with an eclipse, which is rare.

quiz.p: You shine a torch at a ball in a dark room. How much of the ball is lit?
quiz.why: The torch lights the half facing it. The real Earth is the same: half has day and half has night. Picking 'all of it' forgets that light travels in straight lines and cannot reach round the back.
quiz.context: In the torch and ball experiment, a torch is the Sun and a ball is the Earth.

quiz.p: In the torch and ball experiment, the torch stays still. What makes a dot on the ball go from day into night?
quiz.why: Only the ball turned, so the turning made the night. Picking 'moving the torch' is the feeling that the Sun travels. The test kept the torch still to show it does not need to.
quiz.context: In the torch and ball experiment, you stick dots on a ball and turn it in front of a torch.

quiz.p: The Sun seems to rise in the…
quiz.why: The Earth turns from west to east, so the Sun seems to come up in the east. Picking 'west' swaps sunrise and sunset.

quiz.p: From a moving train, the trees seem to move backwards. This is like…
opts: The Sun really moving across the sky
The Sun only seeming to move, because the Earth turns
quiz.why: In both cases, you are the one moving, and still things seem to move the other way. Aryabhata used a boat to explain this in 499 CE. Picking 'the Sun really moving' trusts what it looks like over what is happening.

quiz.p: How long does one spin of the Earth take, from one noon to the next?
quiz.why: One day and one night together take about 24 hours. Picking '12 hours' counts only the daytime. Picking '365 days' mixes up the spin with the trip round the Sun.

quiz.p: Look at the clock showing the time the Sun rose in Mumbai on a day in June. What time is it?
quiz.why: The short hand points at 6 and the long hand points at 12. So it is 6 o'clock. Picking '12 o'clock' reads the long hand as the hour hand. The short hand shows the hour.
quiz.art: A round clock face with the short hand on 6 and the long hand on 12, a small sunrise drawn beside it.

quiz.p: Which sees the sunrise first, Kolkata or Mumbai?
opts: Kolkata, because it is further east
Mumbai, because it is by the sea
Both at the same time, because India has one clock
quiz.why: The Earth turns from west to east, so eastern places turn into the sunlight first. Picking 'the same time' is a common mix-up. India has one clock time, but the Sun does not follow our clock.

quiz.p: It is evening in Bhuj, in Kutch, and the Sun is just setting. In Dong, in Arunachal Pradesh, it is…
quiz.why: Dong is far to the east, so it turned away from the Sun first. Its sunset was about an hour and a half earlier. Picking 'still afternoon' gets the direction backwards.

quiz.p: In 1851, Léon Foucault hung a long pendulum in Paris. Over many hours, its swing seemed to turn round the floor. What did this show?
opts: The Earth turns under the pendulum
quiz.why: A pendulum keeps swinging the same way unless something pushes it sideways. So it was the floor, and the Earth, that turned. Picking 'wind' is a sensible doubt. But the swing turned at the same slow, steady rate, in the same direction, hour after hour, which wind would not do.
quiz.context: A pendulum is a weight on a string or wire that swings to and fro.

quiz.p: Why do the stars seem to circle round Dhruva Tara, the Pole Star, during the night?
opts: The Earth spins, and the Pole Star is above the North Pole
The stars orbit the Pole Star
The Pole Star pulls them round
quiz.why: As the Earth spins, the whole sky seems to turn round the point above the North Pole. Picking 'the stars orbit it' is the same mix-up as thinking the Sun goes round us.

quiz.p: Scientists know for certain exactly how fast the Earth spun when it was first formed.
quiz.why: False. Scientists agree the young Earth spun much faster, so days were shorter. But how short the very first days were is still uncertain.

quiz.p: What do scientists agree is slowly happening to the Earth's spin?
opts: It is speeding up a lot
It is slowly slowing down, so days get a tiny bit longer
quiz.why: The tides rub on the sea floor and act like a gentle brake. A day gets about 2 thousandths of a second longer every 100 years. Picking 'it will stop' turns a tiny change into a scary one. It is far too slow to matter to us.

quiz.p: On Jupiter, a day lasts about 10 hours. On Venus, a day lasts longer than 100 of our days. Why are they so different?
opts: Each planet spins at its own speed
Jupiter is closer to the Sun
quiz.why: The length of a day depends on how fast a planet spins. Jupiter spins fast, and Venus spins very slowly. Picking 'Jupiter is closer' is not true. Jupiter is much further from the Sun than Venus.

quiz.p: A touch-me-not plant was kept in a dark cupboard. Its leaves still opened and closed each day. What does this show?
opts: The plant has its own body clock
quiz.why: The plant kept its daily rhythm with no sunlight, so the timer must be inside it. Jean-Jacques d'Ortous de Mairan found this in 1729. Picking 'light got in' is a good scientist's doubt, and later tests ruled it out.

applications: Clocks and calendars are built on the Earth's spin. One spin is one day.
Sundials, like the giant Samrat Yantra at Jantar Mantar in Jaipur, tell the time with the Sun's shadow.
India's clock time, Indian Standard Time, is set by the Sun over a line near Mirzapur.
Countries set their own time zones so that noon comes roughly in the middle of their day.
Pilots, ships' navigators and travellers once used the Sun and the stars to find their way.
Solar panels make most power around noon, and none at night. Power companies plan for this every day.
Weather forecasters use the Earth's spin to predict which way cyclones will turn.
Rockets are often launched towards the east, to get a free push from the Earth's spin.
Doctors and scientists study body clocks to help night-shift workers, travellers with jet lag and people who cannot sleep.
Astronomers plan when to observe a star by working out when the Earth will turn it into view.
Satellites that photograph the Earth are timed to pass over places at the same sunlit hour each day.
Farmers, fishers and festival calendars across India follow sunrise, sunset and the Moon.

open_questions.q: How fast was the Earth spinning when it was very young?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists agree days were much shorter. But rocks that old are rare, and different studies give different answers.

open_questions.q: Why does Venus spin backwards, so slowly that its day is longer than its year?
open_questions.why_open: Ideas include a giant crash long ago, or the Sun's pull on its thick air. Nobody knows for sure.

open_questions.q: Spinning compared with what? Why does a spinning thing behave as if it is measured against the far-away stars?
open_questions.why_open: Newton, Mach and Einstein all thought about this. Physicists still argue.

open_questions.q: Exactly how do body clocks in different parts of the body stay in step with each other?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know the main genes. How all the clocks in the body talk to each other is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Why do we need to sleep at night at all?
open_questions.why_open: Sleep helps memory, growth and repair. But exactly why almost every animal sleeps is still an open question.

open_questions.q: Why do some days come out a tiny bit shorter, even though the spin is slowing overall?
open_questions.why_open: In recent years, some days were shorter than 24 hours by about a thousandth of a second. Scientists think the Earth's liquid core, the oceans and the air shift the spin a little. The details are still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Why are moths and other insects drawn round street lamps at night?
open_questions.why_open: One idea from 2024 is that insects try to keep their backs towards the brightest light, which used to be the sky. Scientists are still testing it.
