maths.problem: In the shadow stick experiment, the shadow was 40 cm long at 9 in the morning and 8 cm long at 1 in the afternoon. How many centimetres shorter was it at 1 o'clock?
maths.explain: The shadow was 40 cm at 9. It was 8 cm at 1. 40 take away 8 is 32. So the shadow was 32 cm shorter at 1 o'clock. You can check: 8 + 32 = 40.
maths.context: This is about the shadow stick experiment. You stand a stick in the sun and measure the length of its shadow every hour.

chart.title: Shadow length through one day (made-up results)

maths.why_maths: Saying 'the shadow got shorter' is a start. Taking one number from the other tells us exactly how much shorter, so we can compare days and places.

maths.problem: In Pune, the Sun rose at 6 o'clock in the morning and set at 7 o'clock in the evening. How many hours of daylight were there?
maths.explain: From 6 in the morning to 12 noon is 6 hours. From 12 noon to 7 in the evening is 7 hours. 6 + 7 = 13. So there were 13 hours of daylight.
maths.context: This is about the Sunrise and Sunset Diary. You write down the time the Sun rises and sets each day.
maths.why_maths: Sunrise and sunset times are just two clock readings. Working out the time between them tells us how long our town spent in the sunlight that day.

maths.problem: The Earth turns all the way round, 360 degrees, in 24 hours. How many degrees does it turn in 1 hour?
maths.explain: We share 360 degrees equally among 24 hours. 24 × 15 = 360. So 360 divided by 24 is 15. The Earth turns 15 degrees every hour. That is why the Sun seems to move about one and a half fist-widths across the sky every hour, with your arm held out straight.
maths.context: A whole turn is 360 degrees. Degrees are a way of measuring how far something turns. The Earth makes one whole turn in about 24 hours.
maths.why_maths: Knowing how far the Earth turns each hour lets us predict where the Sun will be, and work out the time difference between places.

maths.problem: Read the clock. It shows the time the Sun rose in Dong, Arunachal Pradesh, on a June morning. The Sun rose in Bhuj, Kutch, 2 hours later. What time did it rise in Bhuj?
maths.explain: The clock shows 4:05. The short hand is just past 4, and the long hand is on 1, which means 5 minutes. Add 2 hours: 4:05 becomes 6:05. So the Sun rose in Bhuj at about 6:05.
maths.context: Dong, in the far east of India, turns into the sunlight first. Bhuj, in the far west, turns into it about 2 hours later. India uses one clock time for the whole country.
maths.art: A round clock face with the short hand just past 4 and the long hand on 1, a small sunrise over hills drawn beside it.
maths.why_maths: Reading a clock and adding hours lets us compare sunrise across India, and see the spin of the Earth in the numbers.

maths.problem: Fossil corals show that 400 million years ago a year had about 400 days. Today a year has about 365 days. How many more days did a year have then?
maths.explain: 400 take away 365 is 35. So a year had about 35 more days. The year was about as long as now, but each day was shorter, because the Earth spun faster.
maths.context: Corals grow a thin layer every day, and a pattern every year. Counting the layers in a fossil coral tells us how many days there were in a year long ago.
maths.why_maths: Counting the difference between then and now shows that the Earth's spin has changed, a clue hidden inside a fossil.

roots.context: We have been learning that day and night come from the spinning Earth. Now we ask what that spin tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Night does not fall from the sky. It is the Earth's own shadow, on the half facing away from the Sun. Every evening, the turning Earth carries us into that shadow. So at night, what blocks the Sun is the ground under our feet.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'night falls' and 'the Sun goes down', as if darkness arrived from somewhere or the Sun went away. The Sun never stops shining on the Earth. Night is the shadow side of our own planet, and we turn into it and out of it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the torch and ball experiment, the back of the ball was dark because the ball itself blocked the torch. Just after sunset, the Earth's shadow shows as a dark blue band low in the eastern sky. And when Bhuj has sunset, Dong already has night, under the same Sun.

three.who_am_i: You are not standing still while the sky moves. You ride on a turning Earth, at about 1,500 kilometres an hour, together with everything around you.
three.what_is_life: Every living thing, from a touch-me-not plant to you, has a body clock that keeps time with the Earth's spin.
three.what_is_this_world: There is one Sun and one turning Earth. At every moment it is morning somewhere and night somewhere else.

roots.thread: Day and night look like two opposite things. But they are made by one Sun shining on one ball. Morning in Dong and evening in Bhuj happen at the same moment, on the same Earth, in the same light. The turning only changes which places are in the light. DeepKids believes the world is like this all through: one whole, which looks like separate pieces depending on where you stand in it.

teachings.teaching: The Upanishad speaks of a Sun that no longer rises or sets, but stands alone in the centre. For one who understands this, it says, the Sun does not rise and does not set. For them it is always day.
teachings.link: The Upanishad is speaking about inner understanding, not about astronomy. But it fits what science found in one way. The Sun itself never rises or sets. Rising and setting belong to our place on the turning Earth.

teachings.teaching: Long and short shape each other. High and low lean on each other. Front and back follow one another. Each needs the other to exist.
teachings.link: Day and night are like front and back. A ball lit from one side always has a lit half and a dark half. You cannot have one without the other.

teachings.teaching: A man in a moving boat sees the still trees on the bank moving backwards. In the same way, the still stars seem to move west.
teachings.link: Aryabhata's boat is about science, and also about seeing. What seems to move may be ourselves. Before deciding what is moving, it helps to ask where we are standing.

science.text: The Earth spins once in about 24 hours, and the Sun's daily movement across the sky is only apparent. This is shown by Foucault pendulums, star trails and photos from space.

The Sun and the planets formed from one slowly swirling cloud of gas and dust, about 4.6 billion years ago. Most of the planets' spin comes from that cloud's turning, though giant crashes changed some of it.

other_view.view: Day and night are fully explained by physics: leftover spin from the cloud the Earth formed from, light travelling in straight lines, and a ball blocking it. They see no need for any deeper oneness behind it. That is an honest view, and it is how science works.

practice.title: Feel the ground turn
practice.say: Let's go to a window or terrace at sunset, or stand facing a lamp. Stand still, facing the light, but don't look straight at the Sun. Look at the glow on the buildings or the sky beside it. Don't think of the Sun going down. Imagine the ground under your feet slowly tipping you backwards, away from it. Breathe in slowly. Breathe out slowly. The whole Earth is turning with you. Stay quiet for a moment. Who else is turning with us right now?
practice.kid: Face the setting Sun, or a lamp. Do not look straight at the Sun. Stand very still. Imagine the ground tipping you slowly backwards. Breathe slowly, three times.

how_we_found_out.story: For thousands of years, most people believed that the Earth stood still and the whole sky turned round it once a day. It looked that way, and it felt that way. In 499 CE, the Indian astronomer Aryabhata disagreed. In his book, the Aryabhatiya, he wrote that the Earth turns. He compared us to a man in a moving boat, who sees the trees on the bank slide backwards. Later Indian astronomers, including Brahmagupta, argued against him. In 1543, Copernicus in Poland also wrote that the Earth spins. But for centuries nobody could show the spin directly. In 1851, the French scientist Léon Foucault hung a heavy ball on a 67-metre wire in the Panthéon, a great hall in Paris, and set it swinging. Over the hours, the line of the swing slowly turned round the floor. Nothing was pushing it sideways. The floor, and the whole Earth with it, was turning underneath. Crowds came to watch. Now anyone could see the Earth's spin in a single room.
how_we_found_out.who: Aryabhata (India, 499 CE), Nicolaus Copernicus (Poland, 1543) and Léon Foucault (France, 1851)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The Earth stands still, and the Sun and the stars travel round it every day. Foucault's pendulum showed that it is the floor, and the Earth, that turns.
